So, I hear you took a holiday recently. Yeah, just got back. It was lovely, thanks for asking. Spent a week in Croatia, went sailing and the whole experience was quite enriching. Croatia is great for sailing, isn’t it? The Adriatic is just so calm and clear. Absolutely, and the food was amazing too. But, let me admit it, the main highlight was probably relaxing on the deck and enjoying the scenery. That's the best way to do it. I mean, who needs to be overly vigorous all the time? Someone at work mentioned how beautiful it was this time of year. That sounds amazing! I've never been but from what I've seen, the scenery really is breathtaking. Definitely should do that. Oh, talked to old Bobby the other day down by the butcher’s shop. You know him, don't you? He’s been around forever. What was he up to this time? Speaking of old times, I came across an article about that old Youth hostel you guys went to in Cornwall. Ron and I had a ball there. We met so many interesting people. And the scenery! God, it was beautiful. I never went, but he was always telling me about it. Now it's all about buying and selling houses, huh? Indeed. You see how the kids are coming back to the area and its making property more sought after. And cars? Heard you're thinking of getting a new car, Ron? Oh, maybe. The old banger's doing okay but I wouldn’t mind something that’s a bit easier on the pocket. Cars and houses, they're all part of the hustle and bustle now. Not to mention the buying and selling on eBay. Oh, I bought that old sideboard for the house off eBay a few months ago. Bargain of a lifetime. I still prefer the traditional way of getting things. Going to the shop, seeing it, touching it. Speaking of traditional things, we might see a change in local policy next year after the election. Politics. I've never paid it much mind, but I suppose we should. Could affect public transport if it does get privatized further I still get the paper. It’s something almost gone out of fashion but it’s the real deal. Always good to have multiple sources. Even football news is better in print. You guys still follow the teams? Sure do. I like to hear the commentary with a pint. I've got the kids talking about it at dinner sometimes. My grandkids like to watch the matches too now. Health, that’s another thing. With news about the healthcare system, it’s always a discussion. Can't say it's what we talked about when I was young, but important now.

So tell me about the baby, did he sleep through last night? [Chuckles] Oh, that would be a yes! Well, most of the night at least. Got up twice but that's pretty good for him, really. Just two times! That's fantastic. I'm sure it's so exhausting but also wonderful at the same time. It is, absolutely. I'm still struggling to get my head around breastfeeding. Of course! And they keep offering to come over and help out. Honestly, it's been a huge help already. They're amazing, aren’t they? To be honest, it's been a bit of a juggle but my boss has been understanding about the extra time off I need to help you. You know how we used to explore the little nooks and corners of this house and the garden when we were little? Now you're thinking about baby-proofing every corner. True, that is similar.

Because tomorrow's the day for visiting family perhaps I could do it then no it's got to be today in between work and everything else. So have you got your Ed Sheeran tickets yet? Well, no, they went off sale the minute I had dinner ready but I'm hoping to see one of his neighbors or something now, the concert’s only a month away! Oh, that must be so cool. Speaking of cool, have you heard about the plant exchange our bio class is organizing this term? I had no idea. That sounds fun. Plants are so diverse and keeps changing as you observe them. You ever try to grow succulents? I tried, but they all ended up dying – I think I forgot to water them. Haha yes I did that too with a cactus. But talking about forgetting, did you finish the algebra homework from last week? Yeah, that was tricky. I had to re-watch the video on limits because I didn’t understand it first time. Ugh, me too. It’s like they expect us to be equations experts already. Do you think Mr. Thompson will give us extra time for the test on Thursday? I don’t know, but I hope so. The whole class was struggling in class the other day. But would that clash with the bio project we talked about? Actually, it could tie in. We might design or create something during the club that shows biodiversity or something. Oh that’s a great idea. Our art project for the term is on plants. Maybe we can use stamps from different countries with native plants on them. Exactly! Or use the science club for the natural elements and art for the aesthetic appeal. We should make that our art for the school Christmas fair then. Our art teacher loves interdisciplinary projects. So Grace, today we’ve got quite a packed schedule in Venice. That’s right. Got all of our main sights marked out on the map. We’ve got St. Mark’s Basilica, the Doge’s Palace, and a gondola ride lined up for the afternoon. What else do you think we should do? I think we should definitely include a visit to the Rialto Market. It’s very traditional and it’s always got interesting keepsakes for sale alongside all the fresh food. Yeah, okay. That makes sense. We should check it out. You’ve been here before, have you noticed any changes since then? Well, the city’s always changing in some ways, but it’s still the same old charming self, full of character. What I have noticed is more of an effort to regulate the tourist numbers during peak season, which sometimes makes it a bit more manageable. Good to hear. I’ve heard about the influx of tourists and the challenges that comes with it. I guess it’s a double-edged sword; economically it’s great, but it can overwhelm the city. Exactly. Venice is still the unique, picturesque place we all know and love, but over-tourism is a serious issue they’re working on. Now let’s talk about something more pleasant – like food and drink. I’ve heard that Cicchetti, little plates of food akin to tapas, are a really good thing to try when we’re here, and they have fantastic local wines and Prosecco. Oh, that sounds fantastic! I’m all for that. We should definitely have a good mix of traditional Venetian cuisine and some of those cicchetti. What about some coffee or gelato? The Italian coffee culture is a must-experience. Of course! You can’t say no to Italian coffee, and gelato is a must-have for me after every meal. From cafes like Florian or Quadri, we can catch some good espresso, and after lunch, let’s go for a gelato somewhere local. I’ve got a recommendation for a small place near St. Mark’s Square, they serve the creamiest pistachio ice cream you’ve ever had. That sounds heavenly and pistachio is my favorite. So, we’ve got most of our day planned out. I just want to make sure we’ve got enough time for everything plus some free exploration. What time do you want to start moving?

So I finally got back to the gym. You would not believe how slumped I was feeling. Oh yeah, life can get in the way really quickly isn't it? Really quickly! Especially when you're working and trying to do a bit of everything else. And on top of that, I'm still struggling to actually have a decent holiday. All these trips got cancelled. Right? I wanted to go to Rome and...pfft. Maybe next year. Maybe next year. And what's with this pub you've been wanting me to try with Rachel? Is it still on for the weekend? It is - oh we're planning to go this weekend. It's supposed to be really cool, a bit different from your usual pubs. But Ronan, your ex, won't believe me when I say that it's good. Yeah, he'll just say he's never met me before. Anyway, on the topic of good food - have you tried that new pasta restaurant in town? I haven’t yet. You? I have - it's really nice, but apparently the owner is a bit peculiar about how you're supposed to eat their pasta. Like, I asked for extra parmesan and they told me in all seriousness that if I ate it that way, I’d be offending the dish. I mean, come on! That's so absurd. I guess food and opinions can be very personal. Definitely. But getting side-tracked, anyways, what’s new with your project at work? I noticed a lot of stress. It's been a rollercoaster. Last-minute changes, you know? But I think we'll get there in the end. It’s just a lot to coordinate with all these different teams. Yeah, I know that feeling from when I was co-ordinating events for Bupa. It’s a real juggling act. Speaking of juggling, how have you been sleeping? I heard you've been sleeping with all sorts of things... Yeah. Toys, books, sometimes I even sleep with our childhood onesies. I just find company in things when there's no actual company there. It’s a bit silly but...it's better than insomnia. I know, it's so funny how our needs change over time. I now sleep with a tattered old teddy bear; it’s comforting. It's amazing how we've changed and at the same time, how certain habits or comforts stick.

Well, Uncle Edward, congratulations again on your grandchild being born. Is this your first one abroad? Yes, this is a new experience for me, having family grow outside of the country. It's fascinating to think about the differences between here and, say, France. Have you ever thought about how property, enterprise, land, and bureaucracy work there? Actually, I have. I've heard it's a bit different when it comes to land ownership and regulations, isn't it? Yes, quite different from here, dear. I've been reading up on it. Enterprise is highly encouraged, but there is this balance with the state. It's almost like a dance with bureaucracy at times - which we both know well from our experiences. Exactly! But it must be interesting to see how anarchist groups and bureaucrats interact... Quite the dynamic! And these interactions are surprisingly useful in understanding the history of ideas between Spain, France, and here. For sure. We've had a few French visitors to our local pub lately, and they always have fascinating stories about the quirks of their system. Speaking of quirks, did you hear about the Chichester Cathedral spire falling? Do you remember there was an architect by the name of Porden involved? Ah yes, I do remember that. Terrible, wasn’t it? But isn’t it remarkable how history repeats - or at least certain themes and challenges, like architectural failures, do? That leads me to something local that's been bugging me. Did you hear about our new landlord and the complete failure in managing our housing? We've had arguments over things like bollards and sidewalks, which seems petty but speaks to the bigger issue of communication and respect for the community. Yes, I’ve heard complaints. It’s disheartening to see such disconnection. From my own experience with local housing management, even when I was younger, there was always a sense of… of community. Nowadays, it seems some are more eager to please investors than residents. That truly frustrates me. It’s one of the reasons I’ve been thinking of writing a book about our local history and the changes we’ve seen. I’d almost gone to the British Library for research but maybe soon. Ah, excellent! The British Library is a treasure trove for any researcher. I’ve spent hours there, especially when I was writing about Philip of Spain and Mary Tudor.

So have any of you guys tried the new NBA 2K questions yet? Yeah I played last week. Got the triple-double but my team still lost. Haha, that's always the way! Wait till next week it will be released! True. That's why I'm stuck with this version, but it's still epic. Have you heard about the new DLC? Yeah, they added the Toronto Raptors. Might just cosplay up for Halloween as Kawhi Leonard. The four of them chuckle at the thought. Speaking of cosplay, what's the plan for Comic Con this year? Haven't really thought about it. But my older brother was talking about doing a whole Infinity War ensemble. It'd be so cool. That or a character he loves from Forgotten Realms. I'm more into anime cosplay. I prefer the classics. You know, something like Commissioner Gordon. If I'm being honest, I'm more interested in the gaming panels. What's new with whatever console graphics or the technology behind them? Like, have you taken a look at the developments in VR? It's almost indistinguishable from reality. For real. I couldn't believe my eyes when I tried that VR headset at the tech shop. But it's like 2 GBP per minute lol. Not exactly budget-friendly. Honestly though, I'm more interested in what career paths we should be looking into. Our parents keep asking us what we want to do after sixth form. Same here. My mom keeps on about getting into finance or something. But I'm honestly considering gaming as a career. I'm torn between physics and programming. Both excite me, but I'm not sure if I want to go for engineering or just work in software development. I thought about going for sports journalism because I love writing and sports are my other passion. Maybe you should go for both. Start writing about the tech and the graphics in gaming and sports. Not a bad idea. At this point, their waiter comes over. Excuse me, could we get another round of those spring rolls? They were amazing. And... Do you have any healthier options, maybe like steamed veggies or a salad that's not drowned in oil? Waiter: Of course, sir. They are on our menu as well. Great, thanks. And also, are these at the regular price? Waiter: Yes, they are.

[Looking at Speaker_1] Hi mum, isn't it great now? [Enthusiastically] Oh absolutely, I agree! We’ve made so much progress and now the whole house feels fresh and new. [Excitedly] Yeah! I really like the new layout. All my stuff is much more organized now. [Laughs] Well, I think it’s about time, don’t you? It’s amazing how much we’ve accumulated over the years. [Chiming in] And I think this is a perfect opportunity for us to reflect on the importance of minimalism in our lives - not just in how many things we own but in how we live our daily lives. Technology can be so helpful, but sometimes we lean on it too much. For me, it’s about making sure that we value the things that truly matter - family, experiences, good food, and good times. He turns 16 soon, and while his studies are important, it’s always good to take a break and celebrate. [Excited] Yeah! What are we doing? What about his interests? Does he have any hobbies or a favorite movie, perhaps? [Clapping her hands] Oh, I know! Plus, it’s been a busy term for Jonathan and a bit of a treat will do him good. Can we have a small football tournament in the backyard? Maybe even set up a projector to watch a match afterwards? [Five] That sounds like a plan. As long as we keep things simple and enjoyable. Perhaps a picnic in the garden too, if the weather is good. [Considering] And food. Someone needs to plan the menu. [Looks at Speaker_5] You always do such a good job with that. [Smiling] My pleasure! I’d enjoy doing that. We can make his favorite dishes, maybe even some traditional family recipes to make it special.

Have you decided on your GCSE options yet? Yeah. I’m thinking of doing French, Maths, and Chemistry. That sounds good. I’m thinking of doing the same, but maybe French and English instead of Maths. French and English, right? Yeah, but French is for my hopes of traveling and English is for my blog. You run a blog? I didn't know. Yeah, I just started. It's about book reviews mostly. That's cool! So what about the jobs we're thinking of having when we grow up? I’ve started thinking about it too. I might want to be an environmental scientist or maybe go into law. Really? That's ambitious. I know it seems like a lot right now, but I’ve always wanted to help or protect something. That’s actually pretty admirable. I've been thinking of maybe being a doctor or a scientist too. Yeah? What led you to think about that? I guess it's the idea of helping people. But honestly, sometimes PE scares me a bit. PE, yes! There's one person who could talk about it really well. Oh yeah? Who? There's this one YouTuber that's a PE teacher and she talks about perfecting different techniques. Really? I should check her out. Maybe I’ll learn a few less embarrassing ways of doing things! LOL, for sure! Speaking of embarrassing skills, do you remember that time in clarinet class?  laughs  Oh man, yeah! You thought it was hilarious… I was blushing so badly that day. But you improved a lot, right? Yeah, slowly but surely. Speaking of improvement, have either of you noticed those kids who go to almost every club at school just for the hours of job experience? Ah, yes! They must be planning on being super versatile or wanting to look good for universities. I know one who’s joined like ten clubs. Seriously? Yeah, they must be really committed, which is good, but I wonder if it’s really their thing or just for the CV. They might be interested in all of them, but I can see the value in being involved. Definitely. It’s one of those cases where you either know what you’re interested in or experimenting with possibilities. I guess finding that balance is part of growing up, right? Yeah, and sometimes it’s okay to not have everything figured out just yet.

Ah, I hear that the wildlife in this area has been flourishing lately. I've noticed more birds and even some rabbits around here than I have in years. Oh, yes! I've seen a family of foxes with their kits in our back garden just last week. It's a joy to see. That's wonderful! It's great when urban and wildlife areas co-exist like that. It must be due to the local efforts to preserve habitats, perhaps? Indeed, and it's not just here in East Anglia. I read an article about a town in Somerset where they've managed to restore the local bat population through clever conservation projects. [Chuckles] I used to love watching the bats fly around just after sunset, down by the River Wensum when I was younger. Was a real village feel to it - the old fishermen returning from their days out on the water and all that. The historical aspects of our region are fascinating, aren't they? Everything seems steeped in history here. [Nods] Especially the old buildings and the stories they tell. I remember as a lad, we'd hear tales about the old mills and the industries that once thrived here. These days, with the kids coming along, I find myself diving back into history. They love hearing about the St. John the Baptist Church massacre or the rebellion stories [starts to become more animated], "Hereward the Wake's" resistance against the Normans, even if I simplify it for them. [Laughs] Oh, telling history to kids can be quite the challenge. Shows them empathy and the complexity of the past. I've had my share of getting them interested in it. Last week I talked about [hesitates] "The Green Revolution" and how it impacted rural communities here. Some of them got really engaged. [Chuckles] I just tried to get my grandkids interested in the world wars but they ended up chasing my headphones around the room. [Laughs] Kids, always a challenge! But back to the wildlife and historical narrative, there is this really cool software I stumbled upon that helps create family trees that also includes historical events. Makes these stories feel more tangible and less just dates on a page. That sounds fascinating! Though I must admit, technology has got a bit beyond me most days [laughs]. Can you explain more? It's like a digital scrapbook or family saga complete with pictures, text, and even allows you to connect archival records and personal stories to historical events.

Ah, I hear that your lad did well at school last year. Oh he did, he did. His headmaster even commented on how much he’s improved. Better late than never, isn't that the way now? That’s the spirit, lad. I remember when I was at school, we knew how to work. No gadgetry, no fancy technology, just the basics and a bit of hard work. That’s how it was. But even so, it seems kids today get away with not much. You get the blundering, shambling teachers now. [laughs] Well, maybe they're getting more child-friendly, just trying not to scare them off. And the places of study now! [chuckles] My son’s new school, all modern and shiny inside. Reminds me of a fancy wardrobe more than a place for learning. Ooh, wardrobe, that’s a good one! [passes a plate] Someone should make a joke about that. Like, the new school is more of a fashionable showpiece than an effective learning environment, right? [laughs] Modish, rather than 'modest'. You know the new Stamp delivery person? I swear he thinks the village belongs to him. [laughs] He’ll keep you waiting outside while he studies the map as if he's trying to land a spaceship. Can you believe it? They’re more about taking selfies than actually delivering stuff these days. [chuckles] Or tweeting where the package is instead of actually bringing it to you. And then you’ve got them binge-drinking before the first lesson. Seems to be all the rage now. [singing] "Binge drink and learn, learn and binge drink..." [laughs] Now that's what they should teach in school! [laughs] But seriously, I think the health service’s got a bit of a blind eye on it. They're more focused on phantom hospital beds than on what's really plaguing our youth. Phantom beds indeed! And have you seen the cleaning policy? [scoffs] It’s about as effective as trying to dust an elephant with a feather duster. I mean, I clean my house spotless and then the school sends them home grubby. [shakes head] [chuckles] Someone needs to tell them that a bit of elbow grease goes a long way... or remind them that our generation didn’t fall ill purely from dust. [laughs] I miss the days when a bit of fresh air, a decent diet, and a sense of community made you youth healthier, not worrying about cleaning and germ paranoia.

So tell me about your time in Germany working at those exhibitions. We've all heard your successful career; it sounds like quite an adventure. Oh, it was indeed! I invented and marketed various printing systems. Working at exhibitions was ideal for showing our work to clients, and Germany, as you know, is quite prominent in this industry. Going over there involved a lot of travel and, sometimes, navigating quite a bit of bureaucracy, but it was always worth it. I can imagine. How did you pick up the language? Did you have to extensively learn German or was English sufficient in most professional settings? Well, I started with some basic German – enrolling in an intensive course before my first exhibition – but over time, I relied on my technical knowledge and the fact English is commonly used in the industry. Still, there were moments where language barriers made things challenging. But the Germans are usually very patient and appreciate efforts to speak their language, so it turned into its own little adventure. That's very nice to hear. I've always been interested in how these technical applications get developed and marketed. You must've had to be quite innovative at times. For sure! We worked closely with manufacturers and identified trends early on. Our biggest break was probably when we developed a system for colour correction on photographs that could also print in small runs. It was quite revolutionary at the time and opened up several new markets, not just in Germany but across Europe. Ah, I can see why that would be a game-changer. Did you face much competition? Of course! But we always tried to focus on what set our products apart – quality, durability, ease of use. And showing that at exhibitions helped a lot. Plus, we were always open to feedback and willing to adapt. I think that’s what kept us ahead during those years. More than just selling a product, you were selling an experience, a solution. That approach always seems to win in the end. Exactly. And it wasn’t just the product but understanding the culture, too. Germans value reliability and thoroughness, so we tailored our presentations and customer support to highlight that – it worked well for us. I often think about just how international business has become. It’s such a different world from when we were younger. Indeed! And yet, despite all the technology, the basic principles of good sales and marketing haven’t changed.

So, Dad, did you finish reading that stuff you've got on the effects of global warming? Oh, yes, I've been deep into that book for the past few hours. You know I need to pass the time while driving. It's fascinating, though—some of the things they say about questions we need to start asking ourselves about the way we live make me think a lot. I wish climate change and sustainability were more integrated into our curriculum. It's not about just vocabulary or grammar; language is also about understanding the world you're in. Though, let me tell you, even then, what we see in current English language usage—maybe due to abbreviations or "text talk"—it's changing fast. Exactly! Some people say it's "dumbing us down," or whatever, but it's actually pretty complex. Sure, I've seen that. "Grammar Nazis" or whatever, most of them don't get that while the 'official' rules don't change, how English is used does and has throughout history. Take Old English or Middle English, people would barely understand us using them now. Honestly, as an English student, it's silly to me when people judge others because they use slang or write "there, their, or they're" wrong sometimes. Like, language is for communication, and if it works, it works! Absolutely! If you can get your point across, that's what’s most important. Though, personally, I side eye people who try to use overly complicated words just to show off. "Utilization" instead of "use," unless you're actually in a technical or academic context—nah. True. I love learning about the etymology of words though. Like, did you know "squeamish" originally meant a bit more than just being grossed out? It used to apply to fear or dread, but over time, it narrowed down to just physical disgust. Really? I did not know that. Yeah, and "quinoa"—what's with spelling it all the time? I swear, half these health bloggers can't even get it right. It's "keen-wah," right?

Ah, I hear you've seen some of the latest models from's still have a soft spot for the Land Rover Defender. Oh, talked to old Jim the other day down by the butcher. He got a new Range Rover. I talked to Mary last week, and she thought that house we saw in Walsall was perfect for us. She just can't wait to get a new place and move on from this situation. Mum, I can't believe you did it. I'm so glad we got it back. You would've thought after the holidays it'd be talked about but it took longer than I thought. How did you find it? So I'm telling you; these are the people who would come and visit the holidays when I was a little kid! Oh? You mean the usual cast of characters? I talked to old Bobby the other day down by Surrey, and he was saying the wild winter camping has been improving his mental health dramatically, you know, away from the questions and answers kind of life. That sounds fascinating. As a psychotherapist, I often recommend healthy escapes and hobbies to assist in dealing with stress and I'd be very interested to hear more about how this works for him. Absolutely. You know, it's about reconnecting with nature in its most raw form. There's something therapeutic about facing and battling the elements. It's almost instinctual, just like how humans survived millennia ago before our current civilization. Exactly. Bobby was saying that usually he comes back from these trips with a renewed sense of purpose, clarity in his thinking—it's as if the wilderness has somehow reordered his thoughts. He barely speaks about work or the city problems while on his trips. I've had patients or clients, whatever one prefers to call them, who have benefited from similar experiences. The reduced stimuli and exposure to the different rhythms of the natural world can be incredibly grounding and provide perspective. From my perspective as Director of Studies, I've found that students also really benefit from time spent outdoors, especially in wilderness or camps. It's not just the academic break from screens and books—it's the physical activity, the group dynamics, and experiencing the world outside of the classroom that seems to really help in learning focus and empathy. I'd agree, and I think that's where the benefits seep into how we interact with others too. When you're camping in winter, you're reliant on each other for things like keeping warm or getting through the night, which can build trust and dependence in healthy ways. Right! And Bobby also mentioned something about the stillness and quiet—you know, in the city, there's always noise, but out there, it's just the natural noises that are almost meditative. He mentioned feeling like he can truly relax out there, which he rarely gets to do in his busy work-life routine. That speaks to the importance of slowing down, indeed. And it's remarkable how a change of environment can show us what we're missing when we don't take time to step back and just be present in the moment.

Mummy, mummy, tell us a story again! Yeah, about the one with the dragon and the princess? Sure, do you want the same one as last night? No, the princess didn't get into the castle that time! I like when she says "I am stronger than any dragon" Can we build the dragon and the castle from LEGO? That sounds like a fun idea. We can do that tonight after school. I liked it when everyone was quiet and we were all trying to remember.

Ah, I see you’re enjoying the homemade jam first thing in the morning. Makes me think; these are actually from Jeannie’s fruit farm out in the countryside. Could be an opportunity if anyone with real vision wanted to dive into it. Wouldn’t it be good if those kids interested in architecture or restoration could work on it for them? Definitely. It’s a part of the local history. It could be a great project for someone young with passion.

The conversation turns to a lighter topic as Speaker_3 attempts to bring some levity into the conversation:   "Hey, did you see that video of the cat trying to figure out the cat flap...

It's within foreign affairs but it’s the part of it that deals with digital communications and how governments make their messages and public diplomacy work, really focusing on the digital age. That sounds fascinating and so current. Honestly, I feel like all these current events and global discussions in "The Committee" are probably preparing me for understanding the kinds of issues they might deal with. ", "", etc. Hi sis, talked to you recently. Got some down time today, thought I’d catch up. Hi, lovely to hear from you! Busy week, but catches up sound great. So tell me about that new development. I heard they've started tearing things apart over by the old factory. Yeah, it's been a mess. It's supposed to be these fancy new studios for film production. They're promising all sorts of jobs and improving the area, but it's a right mess at the moment. I used to see those old crates when I was taking students around on tours. Any chance of keeping some of those old buildings as part of it? The developers say that rebuilding keeps it "modern and efficient." I personally think they're just looking to make a quick profit. There was such character in those old factories. As I used to tell my students in our British literature class, those old buildings are like characters themselves. Full of stories and history. It's a shame to just tear them down without even considering that. Exactly! My mate Jimmy used to do some painting inside one of them years ago. He said it was a fantastic backdrop, all these walls with history written on them. That reminds me, have you seen or heard much about the new film? I heard this actor from Liverpool is playing this major role. Yeah, the kid who acted in that short film we saw last year? He's actually doing well in this new one. I wonder if we can do something locally to support film initiatives. Perhaps a workshop or a project for kids who might be interested in acting, filming, or production? That sounds like a great idea! I'd help, and maybe some of my cabbie mates would too. We've had plenty of characters come in over the years. Could be great for PR. Actually, that kind of aligns with what I've been planning for next year's community outreach. Maybe we can integrate film together with art workshops? I'd be all for that. Hell, I think I could even get a few connections through my cabbie world. Someone always knows someone who knows someone. Right, so onto something else - did you ever do any painting or acting yourself? I know you're a taxi driver now, but there’s often so much hidden talent. Acting? Nah, zero interest. Painting though, a bit. I did some little bits when I was younger. Just stuff around the house almost as therapy. Nothing serious.

Oh, did you see that?? That's the third hitchhiker we've passed today and none of them will stop! I don't know if they think our camper is too scary or what. Ha! Yeah and I thought this was supposed to be a fun trip, not some kind of extreme hitch-hiking expedition. But, actually, it's quite interesting, isn't it? I wish we could pick them up, actually, would've been nice to hear their stories. Oh definitely! I've heard loads of great stories from hitch-hikers over the years, you know. It's such a different kind of travelling. I've been riding in groups of hippies, individual backpackers looking for their next thrill, and even a few families. Everyone's got a good tale to tell. Yeah! What's that phrase? "For every minute of quiet contemplation, there's an hour's worth of stories with fellow travellers." Exactly! We're experiencing the travel-as-adventures kind of thing, for sure. And you know what I also find really neat? The different layouts of the countryside. In England, it's so dense and urbanized even if you're in the countryside, but here it's so vast, the roads so sparse. It is beautiful, isn't it? And we can't help but notice how empty it feels sometimes. It's like a different world. Like, where are all the people, you know? It makes me wonder about all the small towns we're passing by; what's the story behind each one? And yet, they're just dots on the map unless you actually dwell in them. Oh, that reminds me of this website we found that kind of mapped out all these quirky little town things you could do. Seems like the Morebrows in the West weren't real, but the Curiosity Café in Tatras National Park is indeed a thing. We should stop there on the way back. Good call! And we should also make sure to grab something to eat at one of the local places. I heard the Zajazd Cisownica near Zubrzyca has incredible food for local prices. If we're lucky we might even take a break there. You want to grab some Świderek and go with the locals? I've heard it's this folklore pancake-like pastry... Ooh yes. I've heard good things. But really, between you and me, we should also figure out if all these expenses seem proportionate to the joy this trip's brought.

So you've just got this new beast from the company? Yep, they asked me to test it out and give them feedback. That looks like it can run even the most demanding apps. You get a lot of memory and processing power with this one? Yeah, 32GB RAM and a top-of-the-line i9 processor. It's a beast. But I was surprised they didn’t add in the latest faster SSD options by default - oh wait! Ah, they have included a hybrid drive, which should be faster than traditional HDDs. What's the deal with hybrid drives these days? Are they as reliable as SSDs? They're more of a middle ground, really. Higher capacity but still faster than HDDs. They use both flash memory and spinning disks. It's cost-effective for mass storage but they might not be as quick for certain tasks as an all-flash setup. Is it like a compromise to keep the price down? I see. Exactly. It's a good compromise for most users, considering we’re not all running intense graphics or 4K video editing jobs all day. True, but the real question is how it handles video rendering or intense gaming sessions? I’ve heard if you're planning to game, going all SSD is the way to go. Yeah, for gaming or video work, it's definitely better. But this setup should handle most productivity tasks without a hitch. Plus, it's upgradable if you need more storage or speed down the line. Upgrading – I remember when we had to deal with these for our school projects back in the day. Yeah, and software took up like 3.5-inch disks back then... Now we just download everything over the internet. And then there's the software side. Are you planning to install any retro or unique software to test this new laptop? Like maybe some retro games to see if it handles them well or.. Actually... I was considering loading up some old DOS games or maybe giving MS-DOS a spin just for kicks. See if it can still handle it. That could be fun. Though, I hope it at least runs them as smoothly as Minecraft on my older laptop. We can always set a YouTube tab going to see if streaming 4K is smooth or if it starts to stutter. Yeah, and maybe I'll fire up one of those GUI-based retro PC emulators, like DOSBox or ScummVM, to see if it can handle some classic point-and-click adventure games.

Oh, did I mention my first year's flatmate was called Amélie; every time we had pancakes, and she slumped out of bed, talked about her chicken and tea-fueled nights, I couldn't help but think of that Chick-fil-A jingle—'Eat more chicken, get questions.' That's totally bizarre. But wait, are you telling me Amélie was addicted to chicken and Earl Grey? Like, a serious addiction? Oh, not addiction... She just really liked chicken and tea, okay? But we had this ritual every Wednesday morning. Pancakes, always with chicken—and for her, always with tea, despite the health implications of early avacado-chicken-tea combos. Well, when I think 'addiction', I think of things that might be a bit more intense than just a lovable quirk, but I do understand where you're coming from. It's... endearing in a weird way. Definitely. It's funny because it was so far from what I ever expected in a university friend. But it shaped our relationship so much. Identity, for her, was very much tied into these comforting rituals. I mean, I'm more of a comfort zone disruptor while for her it's about reinforcing what makes her feel safe and known. Yeah, and now that you mention it, it's similar to how identity can be rooted in specific cultural practices or foods for many people. There's this pull to what feels authentic, right? But does that ever limit you? Oh definitely. Like when I moved abroad to teach English, it was hard to adjust to not having the same kind of tea or the chicken and pancake ritual. Identity crises all around when your comfort foods aren’t the same or available. I get that. When I moved to Poland, I found myself craving those classic British couplets—like cake and tea or fish and chips. But then you realize it's not so much about changing the foods as about changing how you sit with discomfort. Exactly. It’s about building new rituals, new comforts. But it’s funny when you think about identity so much of it is tied into what we do or consume daily—even if it's something as simple as chicken. Right, and that’s why friendships like ours are so important—because they remind you who you were and who you're still discovering. Speaking of friends, did I tell you about our fitness plans?

Mum, Dad, did you hear about the Dorset Steam Fair's online ticket sales started today? I think we should try and buy some beforehand. Oh, the Steam Fair? Yes, but I need to check the dates first isn't it because sometimes I get mixed up. It's usually around the end of May or beginning of June, right? Ah, yes - oh we need to make sure to bring the permit and hope they have designated parking. And what about the weather? Indeed, we’re always trying to save up but this is a family event we look forward to. Plus, they have a lot of activities for the kids. The only issue might be moving around the fair. Perhaps we'll look into that. We could sit together and watch while Dad's on the scooter, that way we can all stay in one spot. Perfect, and I suggest we buy tickets online right away, if we're going to get good prices or availability. Mmm, you're right. Mobility scooter plus tickets for all of us... I hope the prices are reasonable. I dislike overspending. We can share costs or discuss if we need help from you, Mum. You could even book a reduced price ticket for mobility reasons, that's always a good possibility.

Oh, isn't it lovely how something so simple can be so satisfyingly complicated? Speaking of complications, I was just thinking... I've always heard about the quirks of working abroad, but I never really imagined you fitting in as a quintessential British journalist down there. Must have been quite the cultural experience. Almost like every interaction's a little tutorial! So what was this experience like for you? Was everything explained overly—or is that just different communication norms? I'm studying sociocultural differences this term. Oh, over-explanation wasn't the problem; it was often under-explanation. Except for when it came to sports or food—then everyone's an expert, no explanations required. But in work settings, sometimes... I mean, have you guys noticed the American tendency to focus on empathy and "feeling" in professional contexts? It was a bit jarring at first. Speak for yourself! I've worked with chefs in New York, and they don't waste a second with small talk. The kitchen's a hierarchy, plain and simple. If you're slow, you're out. Oh, but that's part of what I mean. For example, if we were discussing a project, they'd want to know how I was feeling about it before talking strategy. It's not necessarily bad, just different from what I expected. Do you think that plays into their tendency to over-explain or emphasize feeling in professional settings? I think so. Growing up with a culture so focused on positive reinforcement, self-esteem, and always finding the good in every situation... it shapes a person's communication style across the board. At first, it can come across as naive or insincere if you're not used to it. But once you understand it's just a different cultural baseline for how relationships work—it becomes endearing.

So tell me about that new book you've been devouring. I have heard so many recommendations; it sounds like it's going to change everything. Oh, it really has. But then he also brings in these meditative, observational aspects that really have you rethinking certain lifestyle choices and values. I've read a lot of creative non-fiction lately, too. And think about it - we've both traveled extensively, but sometimes it's traveling and sometimes it’s just noticing the small details changing around us where we are. Right. I think that's part of what draws me to this book: it's about not just traveling but truly being present, wherever you are. And it's surprising how much we explored the world without truly seeing it. Did the book inspire you to take any action based on this idea of being present or reconsidering certain aspects of your life and priorities?

Ah, George, welcome back to the nest. Thanks John, it's good to be back. You're still carrying on then? Still keeping the tea and biscuits coming. Better here than out in the cold. So how did you and your friends end up going to Manchester this summer? Was it just a spontaneous decision or did you plan it out? Actually, the idea was floating around for a while. First, some of my mates had planned to visit one of them who recently moved there for work, but then a few more decided they wanted to join in, and eventually, we ended up with a solid group. And how was it? It was amazing! We explored the city, we went to those new music venues in the Northern Quarter, had a few drinks at Birch and beyond, and even caught a gig or two. Did you guys try any of the iconic places or go with something more modern? We got a mix, actually. We did the classic Chinese grab on Wilmslow Road—you know, the busiest Chinese takeaway or whatever, it was legendary. But we also tried some trendy ethnic food places that have come up, like that Korean BBQ place near the Printworks. The guy who took the order was hilarious. The way they set it up, with the slow-motion shots and the dramatic music—it's almost a short film. I was wondering who would actually make it into a proper movie the way that advert kind of does. I know, right? I was thinking it would make a great film. Maybe the producers just went: “Right, just slap on some popular music and we’ve got a win!” [laughs] There’s definitely a formula to it. And it works. I noticed my dad was intrigued too. You know how adults are with new restaurant adverts. True. I rolled my eyes but also couldn’t help but enjoy it. Advertising’s changed so much, isn’t it? Definitely. It feels like ads are getting more inventive and storytelling-focused, and it’s engaging even if you aren’t aiming to buy the product just yet. Maybe I should look into how that production was done. Yeah, the quality is getting better each year.

So, you had that hospital appointment again? How was it? Oh, the usual, really. Nothing groundbreaking. The doctor just kind of brushed over the whole thing and then reminded me again about the blood pressure and weight loss. It feels like they just want me to diet right now, as if that's the magic solution. I know that feeling. My sister’s still on about it too. Since her dad passed, we've all noticed she's eating way less. Like, she’s always passing up food, and I worry that she’s not getting enough nutrition. Death just seems to have taken a toll. It really does. I feel like that whole "watch your weight, reduce stress" thing can sometimes be too much after you lose someone. It's hard to focus on yourself when you're still coping. But how’s she doing? I barely see her now. Well, it’s tough. The funeral was… I don’t know, surreal. Seeing everyone there was a bit of a reality check. It feels like everything just kind of grinds to a halt when death comes into play. We did have this huge family discussion about everything. Like, my mum was crying, my dad was expressing grief in his own way, which often means he doesn't talk much, and then my sister was just very upset about food . It was all laid bare. Oh really? Communication can be key, even if it’s all thrown together. For sure. But it’s interesting how everyone deals with grief differently. Some people want to talk about the food and the weight, but for me, it feels like just a surface-level discussion when we should be talking about feelings, right? But it’s just hard, isn’t it? To get everyone to open up? Yeah, it is. It’s like, they’re all trying to process it in their own way. I notice changing habits after something like that. People start taking vitamins, or they suddenly become interested in a new diet fad. I suppose seeking control is understandable. Exactly. I think we all feel a bit lost and powerless when someone dies, and so taking control of little things, like health or diet, can feel helpful. However, it’s also just as important to address the emotions. Clearly, I’m still working on that with my family. It’s like society can be very funny about body image too.

Maybe check out the new exhibit at the museum. Good idea. And it'll save me from having to reorganize the roster for next week if the air quality doesn't improve. Also, did you hear from our friend about that dinner plans this Thursday? Yeah, he sent a WhatsApp. It's still on at 6, so let's make sure we can fit in the time. He said his wife is making her amazing noodles. I'm looking forward to that. She does the best wontons ever. Agreed. That said, it's been a long day. Let's head home and try to get a better breath of air the moment we walk into the flat. Absolutely. I just hope the pollution situation gets under control soon. It's really affecting daily life here. Me too. On a positive note, at least our city is taking more steps towards renewable energy sources. That’s good to hear. Perhaps changing the energy landscape will help with our pollution issues. Hopefully soon. No more walking home with feeling like you've smoked a pack of cigarettes just from being outside for 10 minutes. You know, I always feel like a bit of a pioneer for the green energy cause after these walks. Each step is a tiny act of resistance to the pollution around us. You're a bit of a hero to us all already. Maybe we should start a "pollution-free zone" campaign in the neighborhood. Just imagine a spot with decent air for a breath of fresh air. Only if there’s also decent food and drink at that zone!

Right okay so I'm going to make homemade pastry for these pasties. That's brilliant, will you use suet? Yes, I've got some but I need to work out the ratio for this because it's going to be a vegetarian version. Oh that sounds great! Do you have a recipe? I've got a basic recipe but I may need to adapt it a bit. Suet makes such a difference. Absolutely, and it gives a better texture. You'll need it if you're making traditional pasties. So what's in today's pasties? Today, just vegetables - carrot, sweet potato, onion. No meat in this batch. Ah yes, that's perfect for me. Yeah, I love vegetable pasties too. Let's talk about lunch then since we're on the same topic. What are we doing this Friday? Well, I thought we could go to that new pub that just opened up this side of town and they have a lovely lunchtime menu. That sounds good fun. What do we think about photos? I need some for the department portfolio. Do we have enough stock photos? I remember sending some in before but perhaps we need fresh ones. I can probably take some, especially if we go for a walk in Tunbridges really early to catch the morning light which always looks great in photos. That's a good idea. How about we meet up next Sunday morning if the weather holds? Yes, that'd be perfect. I can come armed with my camera. Good plan. More food - do any of you still watch The Great British Bake-off? Yes, every year. It's such a feel-good show. Absolutely, but I also love a good crime drama. Any recommendations? Well, I've just started watching a series on BBC iPlayer but I don't know if it's what you'd like. It's quite intense. What's it called? "The Trial" with Olivia Colman. I'll definitely check it out. Oh! Did you see that episode of "Kitchen Nightmares" with Gary the chef turning up to help a struggling family-run pub? No, but I love that show. It often gets me teary-eyed with the... The triumphs and the hardships, yes. Anyway, back to pasties now. They smell fantastic already, Tracey. Are we ready to get everything laid out and ready to go once the pastry's rolled out?

So have you seen the new bus route they're planning? No, but I’ve heard talk about it. It seems to be causing some controversy, especially with students. Really? What are they protesting about? Apparently the proposed changes will increase journey times for those relying on buses or walking, and there are rumours about a shortage of buses on the new routes. That is annoying. Cambridge is difficult enough to navigate without changes like that. Yeah, and the university is already expressing concerns about the impact on students and staff. I’ve heard some professors are writing to the council about it. A university press bookshop sounds like a great place to spend an afternoon, though. For sure. Although I prefer the Harvard Book Store in Cambridge over the University Press one. Their selection is better in my opinion. Fair point. Have you ever compared the university systems here and in your area? We seem to have more protests and activism over less serious things here than I’ve seen back home. The ethos of the university world is just different here. Different priorities and a more traditional feel. I suppose so. But sometimes it feels like overemphasis on activism rather than academic rigor. I don’t think it’s a case of one or the other. Many students are highly engaged with their studies but just feel that certain issues need highlighting so changes can be made. True, but there's a line. Being engaged shouldn’t mean neglecting academics. Agreed. Maybe the balance could be better but I think freedom to express concerns is inherently good. True. It’s just something I’ve noticed a lot since moving here. I went to Durham for university; it was a different atmosphere. Durham... I’ve heard that’s a very nice place. It is. I loved it there. Much quieter and easier to focus on studies, from what I remember. So, would you say Cambridge is more… chaotic? Not necessarily chaotic, but definitely more dynamic. Maybe less ordered in some ways but more vibrant. Vibrant, yes. And it keeps it interesting. Sure does. Although sometimes I wish for the simpler bus routes too. Maybe I’ll write to the council on that. In a wider context, such a conversation could evolve into various other topics ranging from shared experiences in universities, life in different parts of the country, work or study-related dilemmas, and so on.

Ah, I can't believe I used to teach mathematics for so long. It feels so long ago. Now I'm more concerned with what will be on the dinner table tonight, wouldn't you say, Susan? You're quite right about that. Still, now that you're retired, you're probably enjoying the chance to cook up a storm whenever you want and not be bound by a bell schedule. That must be lovely. I'm still struggling to get my children to eat anything other than pasta. They seem set for a culinary minimalism keeps coming backwards. Well, tell me about it, darling! Even when I was teaching, I always seemed to need a bit of a maths lesson in getting them to eat their vegetables! [laughs] Well, my little one loves peas - as long as they are still in the shell and she gets to eat them like popcorn. That's innovative. Maybe we need creative maths thinking in the kitchen after all. [chuckles] Exactly. Past generations ate whatever was on their plates because that's what there was. Nowadays? They can be so picky and it's like trying to solve a quadratic equation to get anything good inside them! Speaking of equations, did I ever tell you the story of the time my brother and I were at the local chip shop? Our mother used to give us a five-pound note each week, but instead of spending it all at once, we'd split it into silly little increments in our heads, because if we spent it all we'd have nothing left for the next seven days. That's quite rational thinking for kids that young! I never had to think like that. My parents always made sure we had enough but understanding budgeting from such a young age can be quite a lesson. Indeed it is. I used to insist my students understand percentages when we'd do fun exercises like calculating the amount of money they'd save or lose on grocery items that were on sale. That way it became tangible to them. It's really interesting how our childhood experiences shape our adult choices. Absolutely. For instance, now that I work as a transcriber and editor, I've seen how different dialects and accents affect language comprehension. It reminds me of how my own English language was shaped by family and the places we've lived.

Oh I used to take my first job's passport photos here actually. It's these old buildings, they're still standing. I remember you saying that. It's fascinating how much history is packed around us now, isn't it? It absolutely is. And isn't it lovely how they've integrated the old with the new? Completely. Look at the O2 Arena way back there. That's quite the structure and it doesn't feel out of place at all given its surroundings, at least not in my opinion. No, not really. In fact, it's such a dynamic area today. It's changed so much in our lifetimes. So much. Do you remember when we used to have big family gatherings and we'd all bring so many different drinks to share? It was a nightmare trying to find cups that were big enough for everyone— Oh my god, the struggles with cups and American cups measurements. It was always a major debate between the US measurements and the UK or even just whatever was at hand. And then there were always the different types of cups. We never agreed on anything! Exactly. Nowadays, if I had a choice, I'd totally opt out owning a car. It's so much easier without, especially in London. But family holidays can be tricky, you know? We're planning a trip this year with the family and we're all really excited. Family trips are fantastic but can also be a bit of a logistical nightmare doesn't it? But it's the planning and the anticipation that I kind of love. Absolutely, and if one doesn't drive, the trip planning gets into who takes what, where do we store everything, and so on. But it's worth it. It definitely is. Though it does bring up some interesting questions about our dependence on certain modes of transport and what it means to actually “travel.” You ever think on that? Not often, but sometimes I do. Especially these days when we're talking about sustainable living and all of that. I always take a step back and think, "Is this trip really necessary?" And of course 99% of the time it is with family, you know? It's the worthiness of the experience that I think. If we can make it sustainable and still worthwhile then why not? Exactly.

Speaker_1 :   "Oh look at this rain. It just won't stop, will it? We were supposed to have this outdoor sports day today for the kids and now everything is totally soaked. Do you think we can set up a temporary indoor course for the kids? While you’re dealing with the updates, I can start on that. I might also check if ‘Build-a-Bear’ are open today, in case the kids want some retail therapy. And if swimming lessons are still on, John will probably just enjoy the rain and say ‘Look, Mummy, I’m swimming in the water now!’

Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 while house-sitting in Australia: So, what's the latest with your teaching job? Are you still enjoying it? It's been good, you know. I love working with the kids, but sometimes it feels a bit routine. I've been considering further study to specialize in a certain area. That sounds like a good idea. Career development is always important, especially when you're happy where you are but want to advance. Which area are you looking at? I'm not sure yet, I've been toying with special needs. There's a lot of need for expertise in that field, and it's something that really interests me. That’s a great cause to get behind. I read that in many places, schools need staff trained to support kids with additional needs. And being properly equipped to help those students can make a huge difference. Exactly. But it also requires a lot of patience, understanding, and sometimes, you know, dealing with quite complex situations. It's not for everyone, but I think it's something I'd really like to do. I'm sure you'd be excellent at it. Now, have you thought about how long you plan on staying in this current position? You seem so settled where you are, but the world is full of other opportunities too, right? Yeah, I've been thinking about that too. Maybe in the next five years, I'd like to see if there are possibilities to work in education policy or administration. But that means taking a bit of a risk, moving away from classroom teaching. That makes sense. Sometimes taking that step sideways or even backwards is the best way forward. Have you got any personal goals you're pursuing on the side? Oh, career isn't the only thing I’ve been thinking about. I’ve been meaning to get back into yoga and learning a bit more about photography. Just small personal goals to enrich my life outside of work. That’s fantastic. While you’re dealing with the business side of things, keeping up personal hobbies helps maintain balance, don’t you think? What’s your routine like in Dorchester? Well, it’s busy, but manageable. After work, if I have the energy, a bit of yoga or a walk with the dog. Photography’s more of a weekend thing or during holidays.

So speaking of manners, did you hear about what happened to Laura at work the other day? No, what happened? Right, so she had this client that just wouldn't stop talking about herself, and Laura kept trying to steer the conversation to the actual project and ended up having to wait an hour for the woman to stop talking. That's rude of the woman. I hope Laura had a way to politely set boundaries. You know, sometimes it's really hard to deal with. It's like some people just don't understand social cues or have any sense of waiting for their turn to talk. Yeah, and then there’s online etiquette too, which sometimes feels like it's just as bad but harder to manage because you can't even see each other's body language properly. On that note, did you guys catch that new Pokémon game that just came out? I’m thinking of playing through my childhood again, but it feels weird because it's so different from what it used to be. No, I haven't downloaded it yet. We could have a night and try to catch 'em all again like the good old days. The graphics are still great though, right? Nintendo always knows how to make the games look beautiful even if things evolve. Absolutely. But it’s crazy how much technology has changed since we were kids. Like, I remember when we had to go to the library to research and now all of that is at our fingertips. And speaking of changes, did any of you happen to stop by the local Costa last week? Yeah, they finally installed those new self-service kiosks. It’s both convenient and kind of concerning the future of less human interaction. More convenient for me, less for the staff. I noticed a lot of their staff ended up helping with the machines more than serving coffee. That’s an interesting aspect to consider. I hope they find a way to balance it out so everyone benefits. Yeah, because sometimes I do appreciate some human interaction. Makes you feel like you’re part of the community when you’re chatting with the barista. It does bring up a good point about the kind of society we’re moving towards. Some of us might prefer the personal touch, but others just want their coffee quickly.

Ah, I was at that football match yesterday. Really? Which one? Yeah, tell us about it. It was the Canary's match. They're doing quite well this season. Did they win, though? No, they didn't. It was a draw, but it was an exciting game. The crowd was electric. I've heard of Norwich, of course. I've never been though. Oh, you really should come visit sometime. The medieval city centre is lovely. And the food. I heard about the Norfolk black turkeys, they say they are very good. Absolutely, the black turkeys are among the best. And there’s also places serving big Sunday dinners - proper old-school food, that’s what I like. Speaking of food, I made a blackberry pie yesterday for my lecture on creative writing. Using local ingredients, of course. Local produce is the best. I try and use as much as I can when I'm childminding. The kids love this one bakery that only uses local wheat. I’ve been meaning to start cooking more again. It’s easy to get stuck in teaching and just grab a sandwich or something. [chuckles] I used to cook quite a bit when my wife was alive, but since then, it’s been a struggle, especially after moving back here to Norfolk in retirement. It can be tough without that daily routine. What do you like to cook? Well, I'm quite into stews and casseroles. There’s something about the slow cooking that brings out the flavour. And of course, I make a mean shepherd's pie. Oh, I love shepherd's pie. The best ones are the ones that have a nice crispy top. Do you think if we organised a dinner party, you could make us a dinner for the four of us? [laughs] Oh, that would make me very happy indeed. Though, you might find it’s quite a country-style affair. That’s exactly what we’re looking for! Can we do it next weekend? Well, you’ll need to plan it amongst yourselves then. As long as you can put up with my complete freedom with the menu! That sounds fun. And we could even combine it with some plans we’ve been making for a company night out. A company night out? In Norfolk? Yes! We don’t have to go to London for everything. In fact, Norwich Theatre Royal is quite good.

So, I was thinking about what you said to me last night. Are you really considering dropping out of uni? Yeah, it's just been getting worse. I don't feel like I've learned anything. It's all just really theoretical isn't it? Like, the only things we need to do in modules questions are just kind of like reciting the notes back. But then, in the exam, if you miss a point, that's like, a big chunk of marks. Oh, I know what you mean. And it feels so impractical as well. Like, in most of our modules, it's like, 'Here's a really hypothetical scenario. Let’s discuss it.' Idk, I feel like I’m not developing any skills. Is that what you think? Exactly. It just feels really waste of money and time. Plus, we're all just so stressed. Hence the dirty shoes though. I realized mine are so dirty today and I felt embarrassed when you met my paths out. Dropping out? That's a pretty big decision. What about your family? Are they for it or… My parents are actually pretty supportive of this. I mean, they see how unhappy I am, and they know I’ve always been pretty unhappy at uni. They assumed I’d love it because I liked school so much, but it’s just not the same. It’s not hands on or practical at all. Ah, I see. Like, my A-levels were, you know, hands-on practicals in science, but really, uni is just another way of writing essays and all that. And that’s fine if you want to be like a lecturer or… something that's 99% desk work, but if you want to do anything practical, like build things or work with design or code or even things like hospitality or stuff… Exactly! And, I want to do digital arts. But there’s just no practical stuff in my course. It’s all about theory about history of art, cultural studies and all that but no practical digital art skills. You know, I’ve always thought maybe it's because of where we are. Like, Lancaster University is not known for practical artsy courses, right? If you wanna do hands-on stuff, perhaps you should look elsewhere? Probably. But then, I like it here. The uni itself is lovely and so is the town.

Oh Grace gods it's been too long isn't it since we last met up. Yeah! Definitely unreal. Life just keeps getting busier. Still juggling the project coordination, but I kind of like the variety. It keeps things interesting. You’re still with Pearson? Yeah, part of the marketing team now. I love it actually, it’s very fast paced. But we're always presenting and it can be quite intense during review periods. That makes sense. You'll need to stay flexible, especially with the fast-changing industry. Exactly, and I’ve been wanting to get into more digital marketing, just trying to fit in courses around work. Do you read any good books on that lately? Actually yes, ‘Digital Marketing for Dummies’ is surprisingly helpful. Thanks, I’ll check that out. You liking the new project you started on? What’s it about? It's this big literary heritage project for the city. We’re making digital oracles for old buildings and historical sites so people can scan a QR and get all the information. Should be really cool once it's up and running. You’re always on top of the new trends in publishing. How's the marketing side of that over at Pearson? It's become super key. We’re really pushing our digital platforms like online courses. The team is focused on making sure our users see the benefits of switching to digital in study or professional development contexts. One thing that keeps coming up, and you might know more about this working in the projects sector, is how to make things engaging but not over-loading the user with too much info. That's a tricky one. We've done a lot of research around how less is more in terms of user-facing content, especially for older, less tech-savvy audience segments. We found that simple, clear calls to action couple with small chunks of relevant information are more effective. Also, and this is bonkers, but a very human touch – like having a narrator explain things in a personal, storytelling format can actually increase engagement – it’s counter-intuitive but it seems to work. Ah! That makes sense. I mean, people connect with narratives, right? So the human touch would be a good direction for Pearson’s education content. Yeah, definitely. It’s like...okay, imagine if instead of just showing a text about Kings and Queens, the app instead shows you a personal story of someone related to the king, told through their account.

Are they? Maybe we’ll need to make room soon. eBay’s great for finding rare books or unique items.      Or we could use Amazon too. Thanks for coming over today, particularly since you had a long day. Want a cup of coffee? Oh, yes, please! That sounds fantastic. Especially because this kind of chilling isn't possible often due to my tight work schedule. I wish I could have helped you more at the production meeting earlier. Seems like there was a lot of pressure for improvements. It was a bit stressful, but routine for my role. Management expects us to stay on top of things. However, the part that seemed confusing was the latest update on efficiency protocols. Might have been me too, but those protocols can be overwhelming sometimes. You're managing from a recent graduate spot - do you think the expectations should align better with your experience level? Hmm, I'd say there's a balance. The expectations are high partly because of the field itself, but also possibly because they're trying to push us to adapt and learn fast. However, I do wish there were more mentorship opportunities. That's reasonable. Maybe you could suggest it at the next team meeting? Either way, good on you for navigating it all. I remember when job expectations were simpler, in my time. It really is different now. I sometimes find myself wishing for more structure or defined goals, but then I see how it prompts me to innovate and solve problems creatively. True that! Speaking of which, have you considered plans for this weekend? Could maybe help you plan or grab some free time myself if that's alright. There's nothing specific lined up yet. Except, I've been meaning to visit my grandparents in Lewisham. You know how they are, always asking after my job and expecting me to tell them all about it. Do you think you could maybe come over? For sure, if you want me there. Just need to check my own plans. Though I think a visit to Lewisham could be nice. Thanks! I’ll let you know closer to the time for sure. I have a rough idea when I need to leave so we can make lunch or something if you’re free. Alright, great! I'll be free those days. And if you need any support or just someone to talk to job stuff with, consider me available. I might not know all the technological terms but still, feedback from outside could be useful.

So, I was browsing on Flightradar24 last night and noticed that there are actually still flights operating on Christmas Day. It’s not as empty as you'd think, actually. Really? Are you kidding me? I guess if you're on the other side of the world though, it makes sense... Oh, hell no. Flying on Christmas Day? I'd rather take a boat. I guess some people can't actually spend Christmas at home. Like, service staff, pilots, and stuff. But even so, it must be depressing. Well, some people, like Sarah, prefer not to have to cook for an entire family, so they plan to have Christmas dinner at a London restaurant. Might just sneak down to the café to get a slice of cake, actually. Oh, oh we could do that. And maybe Pick your own boozy hot chocolate. That sounds delicious. You two thinking of a Christmas special menu? That might be a good idea if it's well-priced. Someone should make a few extra quid around the holidays. Maybe a gingerbread latte and mulled apple cider. Those always sell well around this time. And maybe we can bake some mince pies. Traditional British in a way, but people love them. What about a Christmassy cake or tart? Oh, or perhaps a Christmas pudding, even if it is silly to serve in summer. Now that we’re talking about Christmas dessert plans, I heard from some friends in Australia that apparently, it doesn’t get much paler than the concept of "Christmas in summer." Paler, but also different, right? I mean, people have the beach or barbecues. More a barbie, less a bird. Exactly. Anyway, another funny thing from Australia. There's this old adage about confronting wildlife and it being problematic. Like killing something by accident? More like… do you know about the concept of roadkill for dinner? I know it’s not something you'd take pride in, but I’ve heard stories of people being forced to eat roadkill due to circumstances. Or even those anecdotes about people almost upsetting a fox just for fun and realising they’re not that great to deal with if you bother them. Yep. But really, in Australia, people get into accidents with kangaroos and other wildlife quite often on the roads. I know it’s not funny, but... It can’t be the most common conversation starter, yeah.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new car that's almost as fast as our current one but it's got super cool technology like talking navigation and stuff? Oh yeah, I've heard about that. It's got quite a different voice than the other ones, though. It's a kind of Londonish accent if you will. I prefer the smooth and slightly posh one from the other companies. Yeah, I’ve noticed that too. But actually, I've been thinking, does voice tech truly improve how we drive or is it just keeps changing for marketing? Think about it, if it's too silly or distracting, it's a safety issue. Exactly, and I’ve been questioning if the car trends are just a trend like the whole bit about digital dashboard. Everyone went crazy for it, but when you need to adjust the temperature quickly, those screens take ages to properly interact with. Totally, and voice control's the same sometimes. You end up trying to shout commands at the car like Siri on steroids. I prefer it when it's possible to do things quickly and traditionally. Absolutely. Now that we're on this topic, what about the journey to Cambridge? Have we sorted out if we're going with the car or if anyone's assumed we're dividing up? Because if we're in a rush, I thought maybe we could take SpeedySteve [speaker_3’s nickname for a high-speed train] for part of it, but then I'd need to sort parking in advance. True, and regarding the car, if we go with it, we should make sure there's enough space and that we can get decent parking around the city. Or would that slow us down further? For sure, parking and traffic can be a nightmare. Maybe we should check if it's cheaper and more efficient to use the car for just part of the trip? We could, for instance, park it outside the city and take a bus in once we're close. Brilliant idea! We should also consider the time it takes to get a boarding pass for the train and if it’s worth the extra cash for the convenience. Plus if we go in the car, do we have a rough plan on where to take breaks so we don’t tire ourselves out? And have we checked the fuel efficiency?

Did you see that new movie that just came out? No, what’s it called? It’s called "Another Universe". It’s about parallel universes and stuff. Oh right, I heard about it. I didn't know you were into sci-fi though. Me? I'm into anything if it’s well-made. This movie looks like it could be good, though. Parallel universes, right? That’s like some physics stuff, huh? Exactly. It’s actually based on some real concepts from quantum physics. Yeah, but does it go into the maths of it or just the concepts? Probably the concepts. Hollywood doesn’t usually want people to do maths while watching movies. Exactly! But it’s still cool to see how physics ideas make their way into pop culture. So, have you guys heard that new song by this band, One Direction? Oh, I’ve heard they just released something new. I assumed it’s another pop track. I haven’t even checked yet. I’ve been on a grind with school. But music, movies, it’s like a break from all the physics homework I’ve got right now. True dat. But speaking of physics, have you guys started the new unit on energy? No, but I heard it’s getting pretty complex. Complex? That’s an understatement. The moment we jumped into the laws of thermodynamics, I knew the next few weeks were going to be intense. Lmao, exactly right. I was trying to understand the first law and ended up in a bit of a circle with my notes. Wait, the first law of thermodynamics? Isn’t it about energy conservation? Yeah, but it gets tricky when you're trying to apply it. I mean, it’s easy when it’s about a closed system, but when you start looking at real-world scenarios, it can get messy. True, the real-world examples are what almost threw me off. Like, understanding the efficiency of a car engine or how we lose energy as waste heat. Exactly. And don’t even get me started on the second law. You mean entropy and all that? Yeah. Right okay so I think it's my turn to choose first. We've got Articulate. I love this game, it's so fun. Oh, Articulate! And isn't that one of the most enjoyable aspects, trying to get your team to guess a simple word in your own language, right? Exactly! Okay team, my category is... Let's keep guessing. Did we mention hiking? Yes, hiking was a strong contender when the weather allowed. But honestly, that's part of the fun, right? Absolutely, these games are about more than just winning. They're about bringing us together and reviving old hobbies and conversations we've forgotten about. And what better way to do that than while challenging each other in Welsh and English? And it's a delight to see so many pastimes make a comeback through our family game nights.
