Alright then let's start. Whoever draws the highest card of each round plays the first card and sets the suit for the round.      Got it. And remember, if you can't follow suit, you must play a trump card if you have one.      Exactly. After the trick is played, the winner of the trick leads the next one.      Right, so what's the strategy here? You can't just play random cards can you?      Well, you need to consider what cards you have and what you think your opponent might have.  Playing a card       Ah, I just won that trick. You couldn't follow suit there.      I guessed you had high clubs.      I should have seen that coming, I thought you were bluffing.      The art of bluffing is an essential part of the game. But remember, overdoing it can backfire quickly.      Here's a joke about cards – Why did the card player never play cards in the garden? Because all the hearts were planted and the spades were too deep for digging!  Laughter from the group       That's good. I don't often hear card jokes in Welsh.      There are actually quite a few; it's a staple part of playing with family and friends. Often during breaks.  Continuing to play the game, they discuss strategy and share light-hearted anecdotes       Listen, I've dealt with stricter rule books. For us today, let's just enjoy the game and the company.      Definitely. We could sit here all day debating the perfect strategy. But sometimes it's just about the fun and laughter, not winning or losing.      That’s so true. Reminds me of my grandfather teaching me when I was a boy. He said, “The best games are the ones you play with people you love.”      I've had that experience with my students. When we play cards together, it’s not just about learning the game; it's about connections.      Exactly. In the end, it’s not the cards themselves but the memories and conversations made over them that matter most.  They take a short break to share a snack, continuing their light-hearted chatter before returning to the game       Let's play a round where the loser tells a Welsh proverb related to the game or life in general. How's that?      Sounds like fun. Welsh proverbs are so rich and deep.  Continuing to play, they share a mix of wisecracks, strategies, and life advice, woven into playing the game.

Ah, I see you’re from Lincoln as well. I’ve never been though, but I’ve always been fascinated by the language differences within England. Have you ever noticed how much of a North/South divide there still is, linguistically? Absolutely. People from the North often get a fair amount of ribbing because of their dialects and accents, but sometimes it feels like those from the Southeast are dismissed for "talking posh" or losing their regionalisms. [Chuckling] Indeed, very true. The dialects of Lincolnshire, for example, still retain a few unique characteristics. You'll hear words like "coastie" for someone from the coastal regions, which I've not heard elsewhere. I used to teach a class in London and struggled to understand some students from the East End. Fascinating. I've actually spent some time studying the linguistic changes that occurred during the Industrial Revolution. It's incredible how migration and economic shifts can reshape regional dialects over just a few generations. That’s very interesting. I've studied some Spanish because I have family connections there. The regional dialects between Spain and other Spanish speaking countries or even within Spain itself are vast and so different from our own. It makes you realize how much our English dialects are different from each other too, despite being a relatively small country compared to the size of the Spanish-speaking world. Speaking of Spanish, I’ve also had the pleasure. I used to lecture on the politics of language in bilingual regions, particularly focusing on the Basque country. Fascinating case study—how one language can be suppressed or promoted really sheds light on broader societal issues. And China, they have an incredibly broad range of dialects doesn’t they? Mandarin is the official language, but the differences between say, Beijing Mandarin and Cantonese are like night and day, and then you have languages like Shanghainese that are side by side. [Nodding] The variety is staggering. We were just discussing at lunch how much of a challenge translation can be even between dialects of the same language, and then you throw in cultural concepts that don't easily translate... It’s a very good point. Linguistic diversity does more than just reflect cultural differences; it can embody them. I recall a case from when I was teaching international law where interpretation became a matter of contention because of assumptions about the "standard Chinese".

Oh, talked to Hannah recently. Got married! Made me feel old though, you know. Really? Congratulations to her! Must be exciting for her. You know, I was thinking about alphabets the other day when I saw a little kid learning the ABCs. Made me realize how complex language actually is. But on the other hand, maybe that’s the point – it’s supposed to give you context about how things came to be. Sometimes I worry these newer approaches might lose that. For me, it’s about balance. I mean, I teach both ways sometimes – if we’re looking at the American civil rights movement, for example, while the event itself is in the past, the themes of justice and civil rights certainly continue to impact us today, so I do try and connect it to current issues for relevance. But, to your point, perhaps that could go too far and become too focused on the superficial in terms of relevance. For sure. It’s all about striking that balance and making sure the core historical analysis isn’t lost. But it also ties into the bigger discussion about the national curriculum. As someone who works in advertising, I see how easily certain narratives can be shaped by current agendas, and that’s concerning in education, where it’s about a rounded understanding, not just the current flavor of the month. Curriculums seem to move in cycles. I recall when I was in school, everything was about the concepts of industrializing the UK and that sort of economic growth-focused history. Then, by the 80s, it shifted towards more social histories. Maybe now, with these pushes for relevance, we’re just seeing another pendulum swing. It does seem like a swing to me too. And while I think it’s positive to make history more accessible and engaging for students, the concern is the oversimplification or politicization of certain events or eras.

Ah terrible weather we're having now. I remember when it used to be like this but today's no better than when I was young. It's just the way of things. Weather changes but we need to adapt. Speaking of adapting, did you hear about the new furniture on the market? I just got a catalog from a new shop in Harrow. Some of the pieces are quite unique. Yes, I've actually seen that catalog. I bought a few pieces for my own home recently. The craftsmanship is really good, considering it's local. You get value for money. I've always been about the quality of the materials, not just the price. My mother had a lovely wooden table that must have come from ... oh, what was that decade? Was it the sixties or even earlier? Probably. I've still got my grandparents’ old table, which is from before the war. We've decided not to get rid of it even though it's creaky now. That’s a great story. You know, it's these little things that keep history or even just memories alive. Indeed it is. We should learn from both our ancestors and the different experiences in the past. Speaking of which, I attended a rather interesting talk about how the police system in England has developed. Ah, the police. I used to have quite a few run-ins with them back in my day. Honestly though, they were all good blokes deep down. True, they’re just trying to do their job. And jobs were harder to come by back then. I was lucky enough to find work as a childminder for years but I always wondered what my life could have been like if I'd had different opportunities. Opportunities have changed so much, hasn’t it? I started my own business and it’s been a struggle but it’s rewarding. It's all about perseverance and sometimes, just getting a break. And nowadays, you see people changing careers so much in their sixties, which is something I thought I’d be too late for after university. Funny how life works, isn't it? I was never one for university but I followed my father into work and found my own path. We have to make the most of what we've got. It’s the same with the weather; you can't change it, but you can prepare for it.

So how are we going to sort out this little chaos of moving all of Mum's things again? It's just going to take some careful planning, that's all. We need to make sure that we do a proper inventory of what we need to move, and what can be left with our elderly relatives. Makes sense, and I'd really appreciate it if we could do it this weekend before I move to New Zealand. I'd be happy to help, but to be honest, I have to check on some arrangements with the lads first to see if they're available. They've been helping with the moving bit towards Northamptonshire. That's actually a good point. Have you spoken to Uncle Tom and Aunt Sarah about everything? Because remember they said they're amenable to helping out with looking after the garden and handling some of the things in the attic. I haven't spoken to them yet. But between us, their health hasn't been the greatest, has it? For me, it's concerning about shouldering extra responsibilities on them. True enough. I think most of the heavy lifting though, the physical stuff, should actually fall to the lads. We should make that clear when we ask them. What about finances? Have you gotten a better sense of the mortgage rates since the last time we talked? To be honest, I've been in and out of phone calls with the bank all week. Rates are still a bit iffy. I'm hoping we get a bit of a break since we're paying off a larger portion upfront. Fingers crossed, but until then, let's make sure we do things the old-fashioned way—really tight with the budget. No eating out just because, and making the most of what we already have at home. Absolutely, but we can still have fun. Last time I checked, we still have a collection of DVDs from that time we all went through a movies phase. Definitely. I was thinking, maybe we can have a movie night before I fly out. We always have a laugh with those. Sounds like a plan to me. We can show some of the older ones to the kids. They might find it as entertaining as we did in our day. I love that idea, and it'll be a nice way to spend time together one last time before I leave.

So, for tonight’s birthday dinner for Gran, what type of food are we thinking? Right, well, I think we should go with the classic, maybe a roast dinner? She loves meat and vegetables and it seems simple and manageable. That sounds fine to me but considering the heat and the fact that Gran might be fractious I'd prefer to avoid too much heavy stuff. Fractious. That's a good point. Maybe we can do a Thanksgiving style spread? Light meats, salads, sides, just keep it manageable. Yes, that’s a good idea. She likes sweet potatoes as well. Ah, sweet potato mash maybe? Or as a side dish roasted? Exactly. And what about the table arrangement? Do we need special care? Since Gran has dementia, we will need to keep things simple and familiar. So, maybe we arrange the table as she's used to it. Also, symbols or pictures to help her identify her utensils or plates. I'll make sure the labels and markers are ready. That would really be helpful. And do you think we can light candles? It's always a nice touch for birthdays but I'd want to make sure it's safe for her. Absolutely, we’re not going to do anything that could potentially be hazardous. Maybe a small number of LED candles would be ideal. Makes sense. And beverages? Anything specific on that front? She likes her coffee and tea just measured, so those are musts. And, if we can keep it simple with a choice of water, juice, or perhaps a couple glasses of wine for us but definitely keeping it in moderation and respectful to her condition. Right, sure. Also, I think a family photo somewhere visible would be nice. Makes people feel included and often brings a smile. And maybe some music in the background that she enjoys. Yes, and it should be soft. Not loud and overwhelming but something comforting. We could put on something like we used to listen to around the house when we were younger. That would be lovely. Now, onto dessert. Any ideas on that? Well, considering Gran’s love for any type of baking, maybe something like the Great British Bake Off inspired? Yes, maybe a traditional Victoria Sponge, that's her favorite. Perfect, I can check the recipe and make sure we've got all the ingredients. Or, if that's too much trouble, what about just a simple fruit tart?

So, I got my wisdom teeth out yesterday. Oh, gods. How did it go? It was actually okay, I talked to my dentist the whole time. Made it not as scary. That's great! Did they give you a lot of painkillers? Yeah, they gave me some pretty strong stuff. But they said I could still take paracetamol if I needed it. Good. Tablets can be your friend in times like this. Yeah, they really are. Speaking of... my parents are being a bit, um, pushy. They want to check on me all the time, and I just want to do my own stuff. Yeah, that can be tough when you're trying to be independent. Try to communicate your boundaries with them. That's what I'm doing, but sometimes they just don't understand. They mean well, though. They’re probably just worried about you. I know. Sometimes it's hard to see that when they’re hovering. I get it. I'm about to start my own uni course, and my parents have been asking me silly questions about logistics already. Like what? They’re asking if I’ve got my halls sorted, if I’ve registered for all the modules, if I’ve got accommodation... basic stuff, I know, but it feels like they’re still trying to parent me through uni. Exactly! Mine’re always asking if I have my books, and "Do you need help with anything?" doesn’t come across as "I trust you to do the right thing." It's like they're preparing to move back in with us. Ha! Well, I’ve been thinking about moving house again, maybe getting a flatmate. Do you think that's a good idea? For budgeting, definitely. Shared bills are always nice. But it can depend on who you live with. True. I don’t want to end up with someone fussy about the kitchen or something. Yep, that’s always a worry. I mean, I’m relatively easy-going but even so, you’d want to make sure it’s compatible. I know. I've had my fair share of holes and problems in the past with things like that. I’ll have to be careful about choosing the right person. Absolutely. It’s not just about sharing bills but also sharing responsibilities and being considerate. Totally. Anyway, back to my wisdom teeth – the best part is that I get to be a bit picky with what I eat for a while.

Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 :   Background:   It is a Sunday afternoon and Hannah and Sue are home after having been talked about her recent car accident and the various conversations that followed. They are having a quiet time together chatting and catching up.   Sat in the living room, on the sofa:   Speaker_2 : So Hannah, how's the shoulder feeling today? Speaker_1 : It's better, actually. The pain is there, but it isn't as bad as it was when it first happened. The doctor said it might take a few weeks to fully heal, but I'm getting there. Sue: I'm glad to hear that. You had a bit of a scare, didn't you? Sent your heart racing, that's for sure. Hannah: Yeah, I guess you could say that. But the weirdest thing happened after it. One of the nurses at the hospital said the wound looks like it might leave a scar and it kind of... looks like a rabbit? I barely bruised at all, but there's this faint line already showing. Sue: That's not so bad, actually. Scars can be pretty interesting symbols of our experiences. You know, different cultures have different views on scars. In some places, scars are seen as badges of honor. Like if you had a scar from fighting to protect your family or something like that. Hannah: Really? Sue: Definitely. Like in 'Alice in Wonderland', remember how Alice grew and then shrank and sometimes scarred? But they never seemed to be about bad things—they were more about the journey and the adventure. So maybe your scar will tell a story. Hannah: That's a nice way of looking at it. I didn’t realize scars had so much meaning in some cultures. Maybe the scar's okay after all. Sue: Listen, I've been thinking. If you want to, before it fully heals, we can maybe get it photographed and create a little project or something. You know, add it to a piece about personal growth or resilience. Hannah: That's not what I had in mind, but it's kind of cool. I mean, I've always been into photography and art projects. Sue: Exactly! You’ll have something personal and unique. And who knows, it might be a conversation starter. Maybe at school or when you’re older and telling stories about growing up. Hannah: I liked that costume our friend made from Alice in Wonderland.

You wouldn't believe the tea and sympathy I've had from ANON over the weekend. Seems she's now hooked on the fight, even more so after we discussed questions for the planning appeal committee. I'd totally understand. Once you get into the swing of it, it's hard not to be passionate about the cause. Indeed. But it's not just about passion; it's about facts. Remember when we talked about the need for solid research? Look at the planning application for the new wind turbines. What seemed like a simple approval process has uncovered a web of government funding, subsidies, and energy company interests. Exactly. And from what I've observed, the politicians and planning committee members might be swayed by more than just the facts on paper. True. But as teachers, we know how to prepare. We need to equip our group with similar facts and arguments. Show them how the proposed turbines will affect the area, not just in terms of noise and visual impact, but also in terms of the impact on local wildlife and potentially even property value. Exactly. And while we're on this, while the 'alternative energy' banner might sound appealing, at the end of the day, the money trail can't be ignored. Have you seen the amount of government money that goes into subsidies for these energy projects? I mean, we all want 'green' energy, but at what cost really? And to what end, without the proper infrastructure to store and distribute that energy? That's a very good point Sir. It's not just about the money that goes into the subsidies; it's about the research that could be funded if priorities were different. Storing energy efficiently — that should be where more money goes. But I guess the lure of quick fixes and headlines sells better. And yet, Sir, this conversation leads us back to the next big political event in our country — the Scottish referendum. We're changing the energy landscape in Scotland, especially with the emphasis on renewables and independence potentially affecting energy policy more broadly. The referendum is interesting because it highlights the real complexity of our so-called 'energy independence' or zero-carbon goals. The rhetoric is one thing, the actual implementation and the politics behind it are another. Independence might give Scotland more control over its energy sources, but real independence from fossil fuels or even complete freedom from the current energy markets is a whole different ball game.

So Grace, today we'd like to talk about your driving. How is it going? Grace, we've noticed you're still driving with the L-plates. How are you finding the process, dear? You've been driving now for about three months, I believe? Yes, and we're hoping you'll soon be able to take the test. Grace: Erm, yeah, it's okay. I'm just keeps coming across loads of new people in town who don't seem to be aware of the rules. It frustrates me because they're not supposed to be there. Well, that's understandable. But let's remind you to stay calm. It's important to read the situation and react calmly. Exactly. And regarding the test, have you made an appointment yet? Grace: I was thinking of going with [school name] again. They recommended it to me through my school. That's a great choice. They have a good track record. What about the theory? You've been studying diligently, right? Grace: Yes, Mum. I've been going through the Highway Code and doing practice tests. I think I'm ready. Good. Remember to take your time during the test. It's better to take extra seconds than to make a mistake. Grace: I know, but I always get nervous, especially with the manoeuvres. You're not alone in that, dear. But focus on what you've practiced. You can't control how the examiner will react, but you can control how you handle the car. Grace: Thanks for the pep talk, both of you. Always here for you. Now, let's also touch upon car insurance. We thought we should look at getting you a policy as a learner driver. There are insurance policies specifically designed for learner drivers. It's good to start understanding how insurance works and what'll apply to you once you pass. Grace: Yeah, I was thinking of asking Mr. Johnson at the agency for advice. He's always helped me with car issues. Mr. Johnson? He's quite knowledgeable, if a bit of a character. [laughs] Indeed. And while we're on the topic of being prepared, any plans for a holiday next year? Grace: Actually, my friends and I were thinking of going to Spain. Spain will be lovely. But we need to start saving and planning. Yes, budgeting and scheduling any travel is a good idea.

Pa, I was browsing on Facebook yesterday and I came across an app that uses AI to predict the winner of horse races. You would've loved it! Oh really, that sounds quite handy but I'm not sure I'd want to bet on it now, the odds are tricky enough as they are. Exactly! But sometimes it gives tips and says the horse has about a 95% chance of winning. I'm tempted to try it, just for fun I mean, not seriously. Oh, well keeps it interesting I suppose, but always remember to bet wisely and stick to what you can afford to lose. Of course, dear. I just like the excitement of it. Though, if we lived down in Brighton, I suppose we could walk to the races sometimes but from here in Gillingham... And parking in Brighton must be a nightmare? I remember when I worked there, even finding a spot near the track on race days was a challenge. That's true! And the travel from Gillingham to Brighton on race day would be quite a trip. So, I'll stick to the betting pools and this new app for now, see how it goes. Ah good, good. You’re sensible about this, I’m sure it will be fun. Now, how’s university going? It's good, thanks. We're covered quite a bit about healthy eating and nutrition, which has been really interesting. I’m trying to cook more at home as well. You remember how we used to get food from the food bank sometimes when I was little? Yes, yes I do. Times were tough, weren’t they? Makes the progress we’ve made feel quite proud. Yeah, and now I’m planning to make the most of fresh produce from the market, try those new recipes I’ve found, and of course keep an eye on the weather since we’re getting a few cold snaps this time of year. That sounds like a good plan. Cooking from scratch is the healthiest way. We could sit together and cook something new one of these days, what do you think? That would be lovely! I just need to set aside some time. I mean, university keeps me pretty busy but... No rush. And don’t forget to enjoy the process. I used to spend hours in the kitchen just for fun, before job hunting and all that.

So tell me about that Shakespeare thing. You're pretty passionate about's it? Oh, Shakespeare. Yeah, I've always been fascinated by his work, especially Macbeth. But you know who's not? My mum. Why, what did she do? She once tried to make a Macbeth themed dinner party. She thought it'd be a great idea to serve Banquo's Pie and Lady Macbeth's Scones. But then, she realized it didn't quite work out how she thought it would. Oh, that's actually pretty funny. Scones with a twist. I know, right? But then she was talking to her friend down at the bingo, and she started telling her about the Shakespeare themed dinner party. Her friend goes, "Why choose such a dark play? Why not a more lovable one? Try The Taming of the Shrew." Like, "Let's celebrate the husband-as-dressage-master theme with some appetizers." Exactly. But then my mum started saying this line from Taming of the Shrew sarcastically, "What, did you come with friends today? Where be these companions that thou painted?". And then she just paused and said, "I can't believe I'm trying to be Shakespearean in the bingo hall." Your mum's got a good sense of humor. I love it. She does, but then the conversation turned to all the Shakespeare themed 'winning'. Like, if I could inherit Shakespeare's skills in language, it'd be like "winning" at life. Then she goes, "Well, dear, you're more likely to 'win' at the lottery or less likely to lose at golf than inherit his writing skills." Speaking of golf, your family skills are legendary, but your last game was less of a 'winning' moment and more like 'let's see if I can make it to the next hole without losing another golf ball'. True. I rolled a golf ball into a hole for the first time, and my dad was like, "That's so unnatural. Normally, you make it hard for balls to get into holes." Unnatural talent. Exactly. But let's get back to winning. Did you know if my surname were 'Shakespeare', people might think I've inherited those skills or connections? That's one way to sum up the effect of names, I suppose. Exactly! And nicknames can be interesting too. My golf buddies call me "The Great Slasher" though, mostly because I've got a habit of slicing my shots.

So have you seen Grace's new apartment? No, not yet. I've been meaning to swing by but life's been a bit hectic. How's it looking? Oh, it's lovely! Really spacious – way better than her old place. And it's near a park, so she says she loves going for walks at lunchtime. That sounds right up my street. I never had a park near me when I lived in London. Speaking of living arrangements, I'm slowly moving out of my parents' place. They're seeing less and less of me now. [laughs] I’m sure they're getting used to that. I had to have a bit of a chat with mine too. You're officially an adult now, apparently. Yeah, being on your own has its perks, doesn't it? I love being able to cook whatever I want whenever I want. And the mess! [laughs] But seriously, it's freeing. I've been playing around with some new recipes. Keto this, vegan this... it's all quite trendy right now but honestly, who can keep up? I just want to eat without feeling bad about the planet dying because of my choices. [chuckles] Do we, really? I've become super conscious of what I buy too. It's amazing how much of an impact even small changes can have. Speaking of which, have you tried that new cereal shop downtown? They're all about sustainable, eco-friendly production and all that. Oh, I saw that. Yeah, I've been there a couple of times. It's great, but it does come at a price, unfortunately. I mean, if I'm honest, sometimes the budgeting gets me side-tracked from my best intentions. Totally hear you. I try to eat locally and shop at markets when I can but sometimes it's just easier to grab something from the supermarket and call it a day. You know what really bugs me though? People who preach one lifestyle but then do the complete opposite. Like these Instagram influencers who say 'oh I only eat organic' but then they take a photo with a plastic straw in their zero-waste coffee cup. [chuckles] Oh, right. The hypocrites. But honestly, it's hard to know what's real and what's just for show. Yeah. It's all marketing these days. I've been trying to educate myself, though.

Right okay now I'm going to show you around the garden and I've got some things today that I want to talk about. That sounds excellent. You two are always making changes out here. Just trying to make things nice for when questions come in the days and nights isn't it? Indeed, Maud. And aside from that, I've been thinking... of actually looking into getting a TV licence. And why is that dear? Are you planning on putting a TV in your shed? No, no, not at all – but with all the talk about the new programme I heard on – you've heard of it, the one that talks about the cosmos and what not? Yes, the one with the old professor who's always talking about black holes and how we're all nothing more than dust in the wind of time. Exactly! It's quite enlightening. And I've recently been enjoying it on his YouTube lectures. Someone should make a TV show out of what he's doing. Oh it would be quite something. Now come on, show us around your garden then. Right, right. This way. Now, in this part of the garden, I've been planting some new [speaker listens] – let's see, they're called cosmos. They're nice for attracting bees and look pretty as well, especially during an eclipse. They're quite popular for that actually. Eclipse. Yes, doesn't come around that often where we are, but the next one is supposed to be viewable from here, and I want to make sure I have everything set up for it. How are your neighbours? Have they finished putting up that fence? Ah, yes they did. It's done but we are still sorting out the bamboo and the owl box. Owl box? Yes, for the local owls – it's a bit for wildlife. And you know, it’s important to try and support our local species. That's a lovely idea! Now, and this right here [points] is something almost gone out of style – painting. I've started doing a little bit of watercolours, just for myself, trying to capture the garden as the seasons change. You're really getting into all that aren't you? I must say though, it's nice to see that you're keeping busy and active even after... well you know. [laughs] Yes, well, it keeps the mind sharp.

Have you got the voice guide sorted for the trip now? Yeah, I set it up this morning. Going to take us through Nottingham then make a quick stop for food before heading into Birmingham. Good idea, I've actually got a great spot I'd like to try out in Nottingham. It's this little bistro that makes fantastic vegetarian burgers. They're known for using really interesting topping combinations, like the mushroom and truffle – it's supposed to be top-notch. Oh yes, I've heard good things about it too. Nottingham's got a lovely food scene actually. And from there, we can go through Lincolnshire on the way to Birmingham. What do you think about stopping at Lincoln Cathedral? It's supposed to be one of the best in terms of architecture and history. Absolutely, it's been on my list for ages. Plus, it should be a nice break from driving and the kids will love it. Definitely. It's been ages since I’ve been to Lincoln. I’ve heard they’ve done some restoration work too, so the inside may be particularly impressive. Speaking of which, I also really want to show them the streets of Birmingham. There are so many wonderful old buildings and nice little details nobody notices while driving past. Oh, I agree. The Bull Ring area has some funky modern architecture now, but all around it are these gorgeous Victorian and Georgian buildings. I wonder how the old town would’ve contrasted it if the redesigning didn’t happen. You know, I’ve always found it interesting how different regions have different characteristics. Say, the North East where I’m from, people usually lament the lack of variety in public transport. We’re just stuck with buses mostly. Yeah, it’s a really different story there. Here in the south, we’ve got trains and buses more readily available. It’s odd how certain choices in urban planning over the years have shaped what's available. For sure, when I first moved to the south, I thought the public transport was like a dream come true. It took some getting used to for me too when I first moved down here for uni. I went from knowing the vast network of services in Harpenden to needing a map to figure out everything here. Exactly. And houses too, have you ever noticed how housing styles change depending on where you are?

You know, I overheard ANON talking about her birdwatching the other day, and I couldn’t help but think of Mrs. Jenkins. Remember her? The way she could identify any bird song and tell you the type and sometimes even the history behind it. Oh yes, Mrs. Jenkins! She was absolutely amazing with her ears for bird sounds. I used to watch her get out her binoculars and sit for hours just listening to them, and then she'd tell us anything – from the rare visitors passing through to the ones that are more common but equally fascinating. Exactly! She had such a knack for it. And it reminded me, actually, of my old alarm clock. It used to be set to wake me up with a bird song, but I had to switch it off after a few weeks. It was very relaxing in the morning, but it ended up giving me these vivid nightmares about carpets of birds coming for me. Now that’s a strange one! I stick to the traditional buzzing sound myself, but that’s delightful. I often play bird sounds on my phone now while I’m gardening. It makes the entire experience feel more natural and relaxing. It’s odd how something can connect us to nature so distinctively, isn’t it? Like, my grandmother always insisted on feeding birds in her garden, even when we lived in the city. She’d go through heaps of seeds and all sorts, and we’d always end up with a mini aviary in our back garden. I can imagine that. Feeding birds can be quite a commitment but incredibly rewarding, especially if one’s in a place where they can observe them closely. More recently, it’s made me appreciate the variety of birds around here. I noticed a rather confident robin in my garden this week, and it was such a delight. There’s something therapeutic about it, I think. Even just watching them peck on the feeder. Makes me feel a bit of nature is still accessible to us, even with all the concrete around. Absolutely. Speaking of concrete, I finally went to the dentist last week for the first time in years. Oh no, was everything okay? Yes, everything was great, thankfully, no cavities! But what was odd was the dentist himself. He told me about a funny story – he’d had a patient who went in for a nosebleed and realized they had a bird’s nest inside their nostril.

Right! Emma, isn't it? It's lovely to see you! You look fantastic. Oh, thank you! It's been ages, hasn't it? I feel like a lifetime has passed. How have you been? Busy, but good. All very secondary school stuff. But even that keeps changing, loads of new regulations to get my head around. You know, it's funny when you're in a profession for a while, you start thinking you've seen it all, but then trends change. It just like the whole bit about digital platforms for learning. It's good in places, but then you also have to deal with the well-being side of screen time and all that. It's a whole new challenge. That's so true. I mean, thinking about it, my job's gone through similar shifts too. IVF and all that wasn't so common when I started as a social worker or even much discussed. Now, it's a significant part of what I do, helping people through that whole process. That must be tough sometimes, but also so rewarding. I've had friends go through it and the whole journey is so complex, physically, emotionally. It's a lot to manage. It's a rollercoaster, that's for sure, especially for singles wanting to do it on their own as I have. One thing that helps is the support groups, but they're mostly online now, through WhatsApp groups and community platforms. It's made it easier for people to connect across regions, which is great, but also, you see some of the not-so-positive side of people online. The online world - it's both a boon and a curse, right? I mean, personally, whenever I've dealt with anything difficult, like trying to get back into yoga after a while or looking for inspiration to write that book I keep talking about, the internet's been invaluable. You can find everything from how to do a yoga pose to finding that obscure book for research. But people say things online they wouldn't say in real life, don't they? Definitely. It feels like a different part of the brain gets engaged when it comes to the internet. And with everything almost accessible at the touch of a screen, sometimes boundaries get blurred or obliterated. I started a yoga class recently and it's been amazing for my stress levels.

So, how's life been since retirements? Any grand new hobbies now? Ah, you know, it catches up with you. Just trying to keep up with my garden and the grandkids, but my wife is always on my case about this and that. I know the feeling. Teaching is a bit like that keeps you busy, but it has its benefits. Yeah, but I had to deal with a lot of bureaucracy at the end there. Crimes are rising in this area, I hear. It just makes you uneasy. Definitely. Education is big now though—people are making sure their kids get all the help they need. It's good that at least education is taken seriously. But sometimes I wish we could get the local council to focus more on our neighborhood. You ever notice how the old buildings here are getting neglected? Yes, it's sad. I actually met this young team working on a project to restore some of these heritage buildings. They’ve got some good ideas but need more support from local authorities. That’s good to hear. We need more initiatives like that, really. What about politics? You still keep up with that? Well, I try to stay neutral as a teacher, but it’s hard not to get sucked in, really. Health is also another thing we should focus on—the local clinic fees are going up and the NHS is under pressure. Agreed. I used the service a lot more when I was teaching. The staff were always overworked though. Exactly. It’s a worry. But there’s also good news—our local community garden’s really thriving since they got more funding. It’s brought people together and is raising awareness about healthy eating. That’s great! I actually grew a carrot once years ago on my own. Not very successful but I tried. Well, I’m sure if you started again, you’d be better at it. I might take up gardening myself soon—relaxing and good for the mind and health. Yeah, it’s a good idea. Wonder if I could get a patch in that community garden. I could ask. They’re always looking for volunteers and new members. That’d be lovely. You could even get involved with the schools here. They often work with students on projects for the community garden. Exactly, it’s a perfect way to get involved and perhaps guest lecture on language too if they’re interested.

Right okay so I'm going to make homemade pizza first time's a charm I hope. You guys want any toppings? Well maybe some olives wouldn't hurt. Yeah olives and maybe feta. A Greek style pizza sounds good. That’ll work. I'd like some salami and extra cheese though. Fine, fine. Salami and extra cheese then. Speaking of cheese, did you hear that new indie band playing up in Newcastle keeps coming up on my radio. Crazy how local talent can get so big. Newcastle has been quite the hub for music lately, hasn’t it? I’ve been listening to a lot of British indie lately. Yeah, Newcastle’s really vibrant. And Northern indie is just something else—so distinct. Definitely. I’ve also been on this classic movie binge. Watched a few Hitchcock films and also some old black and whites. Right up my alley. Hitchcock's Vertigo was on my radar for a while. Yeah, Vertigo? One of the best. You ever seen it? Oh yeah! The cinematography, the plot—it's all so ahead of its time. It’s interesting how films from back then really stood the test of time. Absolutely. But while we’re on the subject, I saw this one, it’s this bizarre indie film. It’s called "The Lobster." Have you heard of it? I was dubious but ended up loving it. Hmm, I've read about it. It’s got the peculiar twist you might expect from an indie film, right? Yes, it has an odd charm. Reminds me of some of those quirky European films we used to watch at uni. Yeah, quirky is one way to describe it. Now, are we making tea or what? While you talk about movies, I’m changing the subject to something more practical. Good one. I’ll put the kettle on. I also need to pop out to get some olive oil but it can't be delayed because the dough is mixing already. I’ll get the iced tea ready then. This pizza sounds good. Yeah, plus the homemade pizza always tastes better knowing what’s in it. I’ll pour some wine if you want? Nice. Yeah, wine. And while we wait for the pizza, why don’t I see if this new film that just came out on streaming is worth the watch? Sounds like a plan.

So, I hear you've seen some of the latest first-person shooters. What do you think; have they improved anything? Well, they've talked about refining the mission structure and improving visuals but I still think there's room for better exploration and storytelling. I kind of agree. Storyline-wise, it’s starting to feel a bit redundant. Don't you think they're starting to miss out on some genuine character development? Absolutely, and I think it's partly because they're still trying to cram so much into each game. Think about something like Skyrim; it had this massive world, and you really had time to breathe and explore. These new shooters, they feel like you have thirty minutes from getting your mission brief to just trying to survive. I read that one of the developers said they wanted to encourage "streamer-friendly" gameplay. As much as I love watching streams, sometimes I want a game I can just play at my own pace without feeling like I'm trying to create a highlight reel. Did you grab a look at the proposed roadmap for the next few months? I think some of the updates they're rumored to be coming out are actually pretty interesting. Like, finally addressing balance issues that have been keeping the competitive scene on edge. Yeah, that's true. If they can get the weapons and abilities dialed in to the right balance, it could make a big difference. And they keep talking about adding more varied multiplayer modes, perhaps even bringing back some classic maps. I just hope they really focus on quality over quantity. Some of the maps they've released lately feel like they were rushed. I don't want to see them start sacrificing polish for the sake of keeping the community engaged through regular content drops. Speaking of design flaws, have you looked at the career progression in one of these new games? It feels a bit too linear for my taste. Exactly. It's almost like they're trying to create a formulaic experience rather than letting players truly influence their playthrough. This reminds me of working on our new game project. We’re aiming to give players a bit more freedom in how they approach each objective, not just force them along a set path. I love that approach. Games that let you decide your own strategy are often the most replayable and enjoyable.

So, I hear you're planning a big Easter egg hunt for the kids. Yeah, that's the plan. Hopefully they don't get too competitive this time. Last year ended with everyone but one child involved. A bit like the football match, huh? Exactly! The one who wins never believes it's going to get competitive until it's too late. But actually, I've been thinking, we should get involved too. Like, maybe we could have an adult Easter egg hunt with clues leading to our favorite DVDs or books we've been meaning to read. That’s an interesting twist! And what's with this film you've been wanting me to watch with you? Ah, you mean that one about the sports rivalries? I thought you'd enjoy the context. And maybe it’ll even spark some Easter ideas you can use. Oh, right. The Ron Howard film... how does that relate to Easter? Maybe not directly, but it's got a good morale about the thrill of competition and the camaraderie that follows. Plus, it's a fun watch and it might reignite your enthusiasm for football if you're watching the match today. You’re not too distracted, I hope? Stifling a yawn, Do I look really distracted? Just a bit. But seriously, imagine setting up an Easter-themed obstacle course or something. Instead of chocolate eggs, the kids could be racing to find clues leading them through the garden. That’s quite a creative idea doesn’t come across as forced it respects the tradition and the fun aspect. Exactly! Plus, Easter egg hunts are all about the chase, right? So making it more challenging in a fun way just enhances the spirit of the hunt. For the adults, our version could be finding those DVDs or books or even planning our next holiday. Planning a holiday hunt, I like the sound of that. We could even incorporate some of these themes into our future travels. Like, seeking out these hidden local gems, trying out new things. It ties into the spirit of discovery that comes with an Easter hunt or even a football match. It really does. Alright, I’ll consider it. Maybe after the match. I’ll make sure to send you the film now. And don’t worry, if we plan our adult hunt, it will be just as competitive. Count me in.

Oh look at James here he was running around like mad at your birthday party. Oh my goodness yes he was the life and soul of that party. He was literally bouncing off the walls. Still brings a smile to my face. And isn't that one where he got totally covered in cake at his fourth birthday? Yes, and I had to laugh so hard he almost didn't notice! Yes and then there's this one here, Thanksgiving at your place in London. Oh dear, I remember that. The poor turkey almost didn't make it to the table. They even got the dog involved. Yes, I recall being worried about the mess more than anything else. Next is the trip we took to Iceland. Yes he was fascinated by the geysers. I'm pretty sure he enjoyed the hot springs more than anyone else though. He was so determined to soak in every single one. And then there's this one at the cinema, seeing a film about dragons. He was sitting there with his silly glasses on in front of the big screen. Oh yes, and didn't you nearly fall asleep in the front row during the movie? Almost. The movie was good, but he kept on with his endless questions and commentary during the whole thing. I tried to tell him to keep it down but he just couldn’t. And next up, his seventh birthday roller-coaster ride at the funfair. You both did great at the party. He certainly loves his fun. I thought I might lose my stomach with him on the loop-the-loop. And yet he begged us to go again. I believe he has an endless supply of energy. For sure. You know I wish we could have these days back. He's growing up so fast but any chance to relive these moments is great. Me too. They go by so quick. Do you remember the time he insisted on wearing jeans for his grandma's 70th birthday? Oh yes! I made sure to take a photo of that. And it's a picture that always brings a smile when I look at it. He’s a character. Speaking of which, we should start planning some photoshoots now that he’s back from school this week. Good idea. Let's make sure to capture all these new stages too.

So, I was browsing on Amazon yesterday and I came across an eBook that was called “Neighborhood Tables: A Community Cookbook”. It sounds so quaint, doesn't it? Oh, that does sound lovely! Was it by local cooks? Apparently, yes. It features recipes from home cooks around the country, kind of like an updated version of a "Mrs. Beeton" but digital. Ah, I've never bought an eBook but I love the idea. It must be keepsakes for families alongside traditional cookbooks. Exactly! And, you know, it made me think about our own cooking traditions. Do you remember how often we made traditional British dishes like meat pies or toad in the hole? Oh, all the time when I was growing up! They were staples, weren't they? Indeed they were. And during the war, rationing made us creative with very little. Absolutely. I've been thinking of trying to make those for the family. Maybe next Sunday we could have a proper traditional dinner? I'd love that! I've been meaning to try making different types of pies with the kids. And maybe you could bring the ingredients? Certainly, I can do that. Do you also remember the games we used to play outside? Like hopscotch, marbles, skipping rope? Oh, and in Peterborough, we often played 'it's a small world' and all those traditional English games. I'd forgotten about 'it's a small world'. It was great for working out, kind of like an old-fashioned workout, but fun. Those games really built great childhood memories. More than any modern toys, weren't they, for us? Absolutely. We made our own entertainment. And books were quite treasured as well. Do you remember us having books like 'The Railway Children' or 'Enid Blyton's Famous Five'? Oh, Enid Blyton was a staple! And during winter, we often sat inside, knitting or crocheting. I mean, I've seen zero interest from the current generation in such things. True. Though, I've noticed almost gone is the art of traditional crafts like knitting. It's replaced by complete freedom with little focus on handmade items. Well, those were simpler times. But I remember your knitting during Christmas when you were younger. It was adorable to see you trying to make a jumper for... Oh, that was for you, if I recall correctly? It was supposed to be like what mum did for us, but it was a disaster.

Speaker_1 :   "Blimey isn't the weather just lovely today? It's a shame we couldn't have gone for a stroll. You remember when we used to go and walk down the Wensum walk? It was our favourite pastime."   Speaker_2 :   "Lovely indeed. You know, it's funny, those memories. Like when we'd have sandwiches like we are now, chatting away about everything and nothing. Seems like just yesterday we were just like you, out and about, not stuck in here."      "Indeed. Now we're the oldies keeping each other company. Speaking of which, you remember when we thought we'd do all these grand things after retiring? I thought we'd travel, learn something new, maybe even visit those places we always dreamed of. But life got in the way, didn't it?"      "Oh, it certainly did. But it's funny, life's taught us that sometimes it's not about grand gestures or long travels. It's about these small moments. Like right now. Having sandwiches, talking about everything and nothing, that's what life really is, isn't it? Small pleasures, small comforts."      "Small comforts indeed. Speaking of which, did you see that in the paper about the whales that washed up? I couldn't believe it. Such big creatures, and they end up on our shores like that doesn't seem right."      "Well that reminds me of the time we were at the coast and saw all those seagulls. Never understood the fascination with them but there's something about seeing those creatures up close."      "I think it's because we were kids then. Curious about everything. But now, well, it's less about what we see outside and more about what's in here - the warmth, shared memories, and making time for each other despite everything."      "You're right. It's these little chats, like we're having, that are what matter. Gives us a chance to reflect, tell stories... reminds me of when we would watch the news and discuss it afterward. Or those cups of tea we almost always had at this time."      "Absolutely. And I must say, I'm glad we got these new sandwiches cut into those neat little triangles. Always a particular preference of mine. Though I'm not sure how much I care about it right now."      "Oh but that does bring a smile. Tiny things like that, they still have a way of lightening the mood.

So how was your Christmas? It was really nice. You? Oh it was lovely. We just stayed home this year. My sister came over with her two kids, so it was quite the event. That sounds fun. I was out in Kent with family. We had this big Christmas dinner, played games... I bought them all presents too. Presents! I've given up on them. It's such a waste. Really? I thought you loved shopping for others. I used to. But now I just feel like everyone just says they "need" gifts, but they really don't. And then you get stuck with stuff you wouldn't buy yourself, and usually stuff you have to throw away after a while. Oh, completely with you on that! But sometimes... you know, the thought counts, right? For kids especially, I think it's nice to have something to open. I still get excited buying gifts for the kids. They make it all worthwhile. Yeah, for them it's magic. Adults just kind of...pretend. Well, I guess that's the spirit of the season. So, how's work? You must be very busy with the academic year. Yeah, it's been hectic. I've been working on really fun projects with the kids, actually. We did a unit on local history and they wrote these amazing stories. That sounds fantastic! I've been working on developing more outdoor learning activities for my primary school. Trying to get the kids more active and connected with the environment. That’s great. I tried to get my class to write a story about a trip around London, sort of like a couple of years ago before we were all stuck inside. That's a brilliant idea. You could also use it for English language skills, vocab building… Exactly. I want to do more of that. But it’s always about balancing structure with letting kids explore. So, did you both hear about the accident on the A2? Yeah, apparently someone hit a tree or something. Did you know if it delayed anyone? No, I just saw it on the news. They didn't mention delays. My mum often uses that road when she visits me... I'll have to ask her next time she comes. Yeah, better safe than sorry. Speaking of things that are better safe than sorry, have you heard about Mrs. Robinson's new pup?

So, I hear that your sister might be moving out soon, isn't that right? Yeah, she's been thinking about it for ages, but now she's actually got a place lined up. It's a bit of a scary thought because it just means the old routine is gonna change – no more questions at the kitchen table about what she did at work, less mess and noise, but also less company. I know, I'm right there with you. She's been a big help around here especially for my kids when they were younger and now it's just about managing the house. You'll miss her, won’t you? Definitely. She's such a dynamic person and I've really enjoyed her company in our little chats here and there. Does she know what she's looking for in a new place? She's been looking for something that's closer to her work. She's a receptionist so it makes sense. She's also been looking for a nice neighbourhood, she's thinking maybe in the central areas? Mhm. It's tough here for housing though. I heard council housing or even renting decent places is getting so expensive this side of town. Yeah, especially with all the development going on. Where she's found, is the rent affordable? It’s a bit steep, to be honest, but she can manage. It's an apartment, and it's near a park, so nice for walking or perhaps cycling to work. She’s still hoping to find a better price, but as of now, it’s her best bet. And what about working conditions? These days, work life doesn’t seem much easier. Oh, that’s different story. She’s always had to deal with high volumes and stressful situations. Nowadays, the extra stress about getting caught in crime sprees in the city or just the general crowd of the area. But it seems she’s found ways to cope, or maybe it’s just part of her job now. That’s always been tough here in Liverpool, the crime and such. I remember when we first moved in, we had to be a bit more cautious. Yeah, well it's just something we all learn to live with, but it doesn’t mean we like it. And then there are the health issues. With the cold weather and almost gone this way, just being healthy becomes a job in itself.

Oh, yes, planning a trip to Nepal is quite the adventure!      I still can’t believe we’re even discussing it, given our ages, but yes, adventure. You know, it’s funny, I think back to when we were much younger, planning trips seemed so simple. Now, with all the health check-ups and travel insurance, it’s almost a job in itself.      Totally, and oh, I had such a laugh with our conversation about traveling when much younger! My trip to Greece when I was 20 was a disaster - couldn’t even handle the language barrier or the food.      Ah, yes, different times indeed. I think back to my first trip abroad, the sheer wonder of being in a foreign country, not the least worry about gluten-free or vegan food choices!      Oh, yes! Nowadays, isn’t it all about the correct packing list? Water purifiers, first aid kits...      And don't even get me started on finding good sausages in some of those rural areas... or reliable coffee!      Speaking of which, the local Village Shop has been a godsend. Such a difference from the couple of years ago before they revamped it.      Yes, and the Farm Shop’s got everything you need, though a bit more pricey. I’ve been in there for local produce, and it’s worth it for the quality.      Speaking of food, did you hear about the new free school meals system?      Yes, it’s all about more healthy options and catering to dietary needs. I saw that in the local paper.      For families with specific dietary needs, like gluten-free or vegan, it’s a huge help. My child can eat her lunchbox with no worry now.      And the amount of work that goes into it, coordinating all the parents and schools... back in my day, we just sent meat pies and a bit of fruit!      Did anyone offer advice on what to feed a newborn? My sister's just had a baby and is overwhelmed by all the “you mustn’t feed them this before six months” and such.      Your mother-in-law would have something to say about that! Well, there was this one... rumor from the war times about feeding babies and... But maybe let’s stick to what we know for sure!      Yes, can we leave my mother-in-law’s wartime anecdotes for another time? They’re fascinating but not necessarily helpful for modern parenting.

So tell me about your week how was it. To be honest today's been a bit of a relief after all the chaos at work. Oh the usual production dramas then? Yeah exactly. You wouldn't believe the amount of hiccups that popped up out of nowhere. It was just one thing after another and I was seriously close to losing my mind. Sounds like the usual then. I'm right there with you, you never know what's going to happen especially working with so many different stakeholders keeps it interesting I guess. Interesting? It's more along the lines of 'how not to plan a production' every day. But, I suppose it's all part of the adventure. Though, let me tell you, even an adventure can get old if it's the same every day. Yeah, work's been keeping me on my toes too though. It's not so much the project itself - we're working with an international team now, which is nice, broadening my horizons, but the admin side is still the boring-as-can-be part. You two should be careful, you'll end up joining a 'how not to plan a conference' group if it keeps on this scale. Oh, I can tell you, most days are kind of assumed we'll have 'interesting' moments. Like last week’s issue with the catering – we ended up with half the chef’s staff calling in sick and then realizing we had no backups. Crisis management is my second name now. Oh, catering drama, the worst. But you know what, we always pull through somehow. That's the 'event-professional’ badge of honor doesn’t come easy. I can only imagine. For me, it’s the constant requests for 'emergency' one-hour turnarounds on secretarial stuff. Can someone please explain why it’s always a laser printer’s toner that runs out when I’m already slammed? Right? It's like they synchronize it to happen just after I finish the most complicated part of the day. Well, I suppose we should be grateful – boring days are probably the ones we don’t talk about. Alright, but seriously though, planning my sister's birthday party later this month has been a challenge too. Everyone's got an opinion, and apparently, no one agreed with the venue. Birthdays are the worst. Whether it’s coordinating with 8-year-olds or dealing with adult expectations plus now venue approvals – talk about adults wanting to micromanage the party.

So, I was browsing on the local council's website last night. Did you see that today's the last day to submit suggestions for council's development plans for the Moore area? No, I didn't. Is that right? That seems to happen so quickly now, the council’s decision timeline... It kind of sneaks up on you, doesn't it? I mean, we've all been a bit busy but now I think we should make sure we have our say. I was thinking, why don't we start a petition to save the local library? A petition? You think that could make a difference, especially with the council wanting to build more housing? Well, I’m not sure if it’ll change their minds entirely, but at least we’re making our opposition to the demolition clear. And from what I've observed, council members do look at community feedback. If we get enough signatures, maybe they'll reconsider. That's a good idea. But, how would we go about organizing that? And do you know about the council’s procedures for this sort of thing? I'm not sure I've ever filled out a council submission before. Oh, it's quite straightforward. You just have to go to their website, find the right form for a submission on planning, and then write everything out. You can even ask other people at the library if they'd like to sign, spread the word at work... Ah, right. And you'd need to include some sort of proposal for an alternative use or something in there, right? For sure. Suggest a community centre, a museum space, anything. Just to show there are other things that could work besides the library redesigning the area that way. The form will prompt you on what needs to be included, but yeah, it can’t hurt to have some alternative uses in mind. I see, and the council will base their decision at least partially on public feedback, as you mentioned? Exactly. And it's also a good chance to highlight the need for community services. You know, more housing is great, but we can’t lose sight of what makes a community vibrant. Plus, I've heard people say that public libraries are a huge deal when it comes to supporting kids with homework, people on lower incomes, and even just as a quiet place for everyone to go.

[The Jehovah's Witnesses were at my place again this morning, knocking on doors at ten. Can you believe it?] Oh, isn't that the life? Really? Still going strong? I haven't seen them in years. Back then, my kids used to hate getting out of the bath to answer the door. “Don’t you ruin my lovely bubbles, Mum!” they’d yell. [chuckles] Yes, those kids and their priorities. Anyway, I told them this time we weren’t interested. I had to be polite, of course. What else can you do? Oh yes. Jehovah’s Witnesses. Always polite, but sometimes persistent. My brother was actually one of them before he married—ended up making the transition quite gracefully to say the least. Did he? That’s interesting. I met a nice one once. Really nice chap, but rigid as hell about things. But good people, just misguided in my opinion. I never understood it, to be honest. So restrictive. But hey, if that’s what they want. I’ve voted Conservative pretty much all my life, though I might sway this time. The way they’re handling things is a bit concerning. [nods] I used to vote Labour, but now? I wouldn’t know. The whole system seems broken to me. Broken isn’t the word. [pauses to take a bite of her meal] I mean, have you seen the taxes? Like, why am I paying so much for something that clearly isn’t working properly? The only thing certain is that whoever we vote for, we’ll still be paying through the nose. Right. [laughs] [chuckles] At least we can agree on something! You know, village characters can be quirky. There’s Mrs. Jenkins next door, always complaining about the parking at the coast when she actually never goes. Oh, I know her. She's always eager to share her opinions about everyone and everything in the village. But, truly, she’s harmless. And then there's Tom at the pub. Again and again about the lack of parking. Tom almost makes it sound like the world’s going to end because you can’t park near the door if you’re driving a van. Well, I can sort of understand his point. Trying to get past all the cars in the summer is a nightmare. But his solution? More parking spaces that just clog up the whole area further...no.

', '', '', and '': Oh, yes, we need to get new logs for the burner. I totally agree, the house can get chilly without it. And I hope I can help with the upholstering for your chairs during my visit. Are you still using the same fabric? Actually, I'm considering getting something different – maybe a more modern fabric. But I haven't decided yet. Speaking of new things, how was your trip from Tokyo? Was it as fast as they say? Yes, it was incredible. The trains are so efficient and comfortable. We loved looking out the windows at the rice fields. And the people are so polite. It's very different from Britain in that regard. Absolutely! Your favourite, Dad. I saved it specially. Now about next door neighbours... the new ones. Seems quiet from what I’ve seen. Speaking of which, what do you both think of the ideas about work having a more family-friendly policy? I’ve seen some examples that are quite encouraging.

Ah, the cost of buying a house these days. You know, it's ridiculous. I've just heard the prices have skyrocketed in Norfolk, again! Oh, absolutely. But have you tried navigating those roads out here with a newbie Sat Nav? I'm still struggling to get the hang of it. Oh, I've got that keeps changing its mind on me. Says turn left, I end up right back where I started. Ha! These gadgets, they're more trouble than they're worth. Though, let me tell you, even trying to get the TV remote to work on some of these newer sets is a nightmare. Exactly! One button does five different things! I sometimes wonder if they deliberately make them so complicated. Back in my day, TVs had like two buttons - on and off. Simple. And recycling! Now that's something worth complaining about. One moment they say plastic, then no, not that plastic. Paper's okay, but not if it's got color on it. What's the deal? I heard it's the ink, can't process the color. But honestly, it's become so confusing. Can't remember what can and can't go in, especially after moving from London where it was simpler. It's all about the tax and all that, isn't it? Governments need their money somehow. Well, and then the taxes on the house itself, after buying it! You'd think you'd own it after paying so much, but no, recurring costs left and right. Oh, the pension schemes! One day they're safe, the next they say we might not get as much as promised. I've been looking into some alternatives, but you can't beat the security of having your pension set up, even if it's less now. I'm sure in another 10 years, we'll be talking about another overhaul. Politics plays a big role in all this, doesn't it? Politics and health services. My sister had an appointment almost a week ago, still hasn't gotten seen. I know, it's frustrating. So okay I mean money laundering. I don't think I fully understand how that works. Can you explain it to me? Well it's essentially using financial transactions to make money from criminal activity look legitimate. It's complicated, really, but think of it like this: if you've got dodgy income, you can't just put it in the bank and call it a day, right? So you get into real estate, stocks, businesses - anything that you can ruin actually - and then you make it look like profits from that. Which is why it's so hard to catch, because it's not just about following the money, it's about proving those transactions are a façade for criminal activity. Oh, I see. It's like masking a crime with financial operations. Yeah, exactly. And sometimes it’s really simple, sometimes it’s really sophisticated. And the thing is, usually the ones that get caught are the ones doing it simple and obvious. But how does the... how does the actual money get moved around? I mean, doesn't it get flagged at some point? Sometimes it does, but often it's done through a series of small transactions, or maybe they use shell companies or off-shore accounts. These transactions are disguised to look like normal business dealings, but the 'business' doesn't actually exist or isn't as substantial as it seems. It's really hard for us in the banking sector to notice unless there's something very suspicious about the activity – which is why monitoring systems are so important. And in your work, how do you help prevent it? Well, it's a bit of a cat and mouse game, really. The criminals are always trying to find the next loophole or the next way to avoid detection. So, we collaborate closely with law enforcement agencies, the FCA , and other banks to share information and watch for patterns of suspicious activity. For example, if we see a business making lots of transactions but seems to have very few employees or operations to back it up, that's a red flag. Right, and increasingly we're using AI and machine learning to analyze these patterns because sometimes it's too complex for humans to catch. I can't imagine how stressful that job must be. Constantly looking over your shoulder for the next potential scam. It can be, but it’s also very rewarding.
